utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Members of the public who wish to testify may do so either through Zoom or in person.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Those wishing to testify by Zoom must register online at New York City Council's website at www.council.nyc.gov slash land use to sign up.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: For those of you here with us in person, if you registered online in advance, please be sure to see one of the sergeant at arms to prepare and submit a speaker's card.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We will limit public testimony to two minutes per witness.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: If you have additional testimony or if you have written testimony you would like to submit, we ask you to please email it to landusetestimony at council.nyc.gov.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And please include the phrase oversight mayor's housing plan in the subject line of your email.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Lastly, I want to remind everyone that this is a government proceeding and decorum must be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Members of the public are asked not to speak during the meeting unless you are testifying.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who are called to testify and no video recording or photography is allowed.

chapters.summary: He notes agreement on need to increase housing, describes plan's goal of 200,000 new affordable units as part of 700,000 total units, a rate not seen in 100 years.
chapters.title: Chair Riley states goals of Block-by-Block plan

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Across government and private sector, we all agree that New York City must aggressively increase the production of housing and affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The goal of the block-by-block plan are bold and extremely ambitious.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: 200,000 new affordable units as a part of 700,000 total new units over the next decade.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: This represents more housing at a faster rate than New York City has produced in over 100 years.

chapters.summary: He says the administration cannot achieve the goals alone, the council is a partner, but details on how HPD and DCP will achieve numbers are absent.
chapters.title: Chair Riley calls for partnership and details from administration

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The administration alone cannot achieve this rate of housing production.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And I want to remind you today, despite a narrative that too often pits the council against the administration, we are your partners and a group of elected officials who best know the communities we were elected to represent.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And we can effectively help you to achieve the goals laid out in this plan.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Details on how HPD and DCP intend to realistically achieve these numbers remain absent.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We're ready to roll up our sleeves, engage on specifics, and do what government does best, which is set the stage for sustainable community development that meets the larger needs of the city.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: while remaining respectful and inclusive of everyone who calls New York City home.

chapters.summary: He notes housing cannot be isolated; needs jobs, transit, open space, schools. Data shows city-led rezonings produced three times more housing than private applications.
chapters.title: Chair Riley emphasizes infrastructure and proactive planning

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So far in the press and at events, we've heard more about the efforts to fast-track developer applications than we've heard about the planning needed to support new housing.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Housing cannot be thought of just in isolation.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Successful housing is supported by access to jobs, transportation, open space, schools, libraries, grocery stores, and other needed physical infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The data shows that from 2010 to 2020, city-led neighborhood rezonings were responsible for nearly three times more new housing units than private development applications.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: This council, with leadership from Speaker Mendes and myself, has been loud and clear about the benefits of proactive planning,

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: engaging with communities on the ground, and doing the hard work of understanding their needs and identifying their investments to support good growth and quality development.

chapters.summary: He mentions council initiatives in Bay Ridge, Staten Island's North Shore, Park Webster in the Bronx, and the East New York Neighborhood Plan which produced 6,000 units, over 50% affordable, with city investments.
chapters.title: Chair Riley highlights Bay Ridge, Staten Island, and East New York plans

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We are doing the work as shown by the Council's initiative in Bay Ridge, Staten Island's North Shore, and in Park Webster's section of the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We know that DCP understands the value of community engagement and neighborhood rezoning that provided the needed local investment along with new housing.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Recently, DCP has promoted the example of the East New York Neighborhood Plan.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: In the 10 years since the plan was approved,

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: prove over 6,000 units of housing has been built, more than 50% affordable,

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: alongside hundreds of millions of dollars of city investments for neighborhood improvements, including new school seats, improved parks and open space facilities, and other critical infrastructure needed.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The council was proud to partner on this neighborhood rezoning, which represents the success that can be achieved through proactive neighborhood planning.

chapters.summary: He says housing will not be created unless we move together, and asks when details will be available, how communities can participate, and what role neighborhood planning will play.
chapters.title: Chair Riley questions fast-track details and community engagement

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We all want to move fast, but the housing our constituents need will not be created unless we move together and in the same direction.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Creating healthy, diverse communities take time, investment, and meaningful engagement.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And so while I applaud the vision and the goals of the mayor's block-by-block plan and want the administration to be successful, there are a lot of questions that remain.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: When will we start seeing the details of how DCP and HPD intend to build more affordable housing in the fast-track districts?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: How can communities in targeted fast-track areas learn about and participate in any of these efforts?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Is there a vision for planning with communities for an affordable and, most importantly, livable New York City?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: What is the role of neighborhood planning in this administration?

chapters.summary: He asks if HPD will build homeownership and family-sized units, and what the administration will do to secure sustained funding, noting we cannot focus only on taxing the rich or building over rail yards.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks about homeownership and state/federal funding

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Will HPD work to build the kind of housing that New Yorkers tell us they want, like opportunities for home ownership and family-sized units, or simply prioritize the bottom line, total count of a family?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: What will the administration do to work with partners at the state and federal level to secure sustained funding for infrastructure and housing?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We cannot focus only on taxing the rich or building over rail yards.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The most populous city in the country needs all hands on deck opposed to solving the affordability crisis.

chapters.summary: He says there have been no updates since May, DCP has not been forthcoming with micro plans, HPD has not explained financial tools, and details matter.
chapters.title: Chair Riley criticizes lack of updates on Block-by-Block proposals

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Beyond these larger questions, I have specific questions about the initiatives in the mayor's plan, and I hope we can start to fill some of those information gaps today.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: There have been no updates on many of the block-by-block proposals since the plan released in May.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: DCP has not been forthcoming with the micro plans, and HPD...

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Has not told us how they plan to expand their financial tools.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The details matter, and we are here to tease them out.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And I want to be sure that the recently adopted procedural tools don't paper over the needed for planning and community engagement.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: To ensure local needs are met, and that all agencies that contribute to the development of our city can be held accountable by future generations for the way in which we set our transformed New York City.

chapters.summary: He says the objective is to expedite housing while supporting communities, and how, what, and where we build will determine future success.
chapters.title: Chair Riley concludes opening statement on housing goals

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So the objective is clear today, is to start the conversation about how to expedite the construction of housing while supporting our existing communities.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We cannot lose sight of the fact that building new affordable housing is critical for New York City to thrive, but is not sufficient by itself.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: How we build.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: What we build and where we build will determine the future success of our communities and of the city.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Riley and distinguished members of the Land Use Committee.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I'm Cydia Sherman, Chair of the City Planning Commission and Director of the New York City Department of Planning.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I'm joined here today by Michael Sandler, Deputy Commissioner for the Office of Neighborhood Strategies at HPD, as well as my colleagues from DCP, including Executive Director Edith Su Chen.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you for giving us the opportunity to speak with you today.

chapters.summary: He notes his previous testimony in March, and that seven months later, the focus remains on unlocking housing, streamlining, and planning for a fairer city.
chapters.title: Chair Sherman recaps DCP focus on housing crisis

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: When I last testified before you, I was six days into my role at the Department of City Planning.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: At that time, in March, I spoke about the urgency of our city's housing crisis and what it requires of us at DCP.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Unlocking significantly more housing across neighborhoods, streamlining how we work to deliver homes faster, and planning for a fairer, more equitable city.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Seven months later, I can confirm that this has remained the focus of our work.

chapters.summary: He says Mayor Mamdani released the plan, an all-of-the-above approach, and DCP is translating it into action.
chapters.title: Chair Sherman describes Block by Block plan and DCP's role

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Earlier this year, Mayor Mandani released Block by Block, the Block by Block housing plan, which takes an all-of-the-above approach to tackling our housing crisis,

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: combining ambitious affordable housing production goals with investments in public housing, new tools to protect tenants, support for homeownership, and much more.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: At City Planning, along with our partners at HPD, we are translating that vision into action on many fronts.

chapters.summary: He mentions advancing plans along White Plains Road, McDonald's Avenue, and Coney Island Avenue, and developing a citywide transit-oriented development initiative.
chapters.title: Chair Sherman details neighborhood planning and transit-oriented development

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: First, we are working to create more housing choices in more parts of the city.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We have rapidly advanced neighborhood planning efforts along White Plains Road in the Bronx and McDonald's Avenue and Coney Island Avenue in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Working closely with community and city council partners like Chair Riley

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: to develop comprehensive plans that update outdated zoning, create more housing, require permanent affordability, support local businesses, and deliver needed investments.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We greatly appreciate the Council's collaboration and partnership in these efforts.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We are also developing a citywide transit-oriented development initiative.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We have one of the world's most extensive subway systems, and it is the lifeblood of our city.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But in too many places, restrictive zoning limits housing, even directly next to subway stations.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: That means fewer homes near transit, longer commutes, and less access to jobs, schools, services, and opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Through this initiative, we can fix outdated rules, expand housing opportunity, and require affordability so more New Yorkers across all income levels can live close to the transit system they rely on.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: As the proposal takes shape, we look forward to engaging closely with the council and working together to build the support needed to move forward.

chapters.summary: He describes streamlining housing proposals, state reforms to SEQRA, reducing pre-certification from two years to six months, and a Linden Place project reaching review a year earlier.
chapters.title: Chair Sherman outlines SPEED initiative and pre-certification improvements

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Second, we're focused on streamlining how we work to deliver housing at speed.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: As I know our council colleagues agree, government must work deliberately and rigorously, but added processes and unnecessary delay has real consequences.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: When an affordable apartment is delayed,

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: It means a family spends another year doubled up with relatives, another year commuting long distances, another year without a stable home.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: When a project becomes more expensive to build, it means tenants pay more in rent.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And this doesn't even account for housing projects that never materialized to begin with.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Through Mayor Mandani's SPEED initiative, we are streamlining how housing proposals move through city government.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Recent state reforms to SECRA created a window for significant improvements, and we are taking additional steps this fall to bring qualified housing projects through pre-certification in approximately six months down from roughly two years.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We have already worked hard to identify projects in our pipeline that meet the secret exemption and can reach public review faster.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: One recent project on Linden Place in Flushing, Queens, reached review nearly an entire year earlier.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: These time savings don't simply affect project timelines.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: They improve people's lives.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Every home we can deliver faster is a New Yorker who gets in that home sooner.

chapters.summary: He mentions the inaugural Fair Housing Growth Strategy, the Affordable Housing Fast Track with 12 districts, and the goal to expand housing choices.
chapters.title: Chair Sherman presents Fair Housing Growth Strategy and Fast Track

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Third, we are working to make housing growth fairer and more equitable.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: This month, together with HPD, we released the inaugural Fair Housing Growth Strategy, a council-mandated assessment of our housing shortage and framework for meeting that need in a fair and equitable way.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Fundamentally, the goal is for New Yorkers of all incomes and backgrounds to have more choices about where they live in the city.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And we're grateful to the council for its leadership in it.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: establishing this important framework.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: That same vision underlies the Affordable Housing Fast Track, one of the new tools voters approved last November.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: The 12 Fast Track districts we announced earlier this month represent roughly 20% of the city's districts, but produce just 1% of the city's affordable housing over the last five years.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We cannot solve a citywide housing crisis by relying on the same handful of neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: By helping affordable housing move forward where production has lagged, the Fast Track will expand housing choices, address entrenched patterns of unbalanced growth, and help create a fairer, more affordable city.

chapters.summary: He mentions census, city map, waterfronts, industrial areas, community boards, and looks forward to continued partnership with the council.
chapters.title: Chair Sherman highlights other DCP priorities and collaboration

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But housing is only one part of city planning's agenda.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Our team remains focused on supporting the 2030 census, modernizing the city map and address assignment system,

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: planning for resilient waterfronts and thriving industrial and commercial areas, improving how we engage and support community boards, and providing data and insight that can help guide decisions across city government.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And of course, none of this work happens in isolation.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: When I appeared before you in March, I said that I looked forward to a strong and collaborative relationship with the council.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And we know that meeting the needs of New Yorkers will require all of us working together.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: The affordability crisis remains profound.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But over the last several months, we have put new tools in place, launched ambitious planning efforts, and begun changing the way government works so that we can deliver more effectively.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: There is so much more work ahead, and we look forward to continuing it all in partnership with you.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you, and I'm happy to answer any questions.

chapters.summary: He asks if DCP is studying conditions in the 12 affected districts to identify opportunities for upzoning that produce affordable housing.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks if DCP is studying fast-track districts for upzoning

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I'm going to start with the first round of questions, then I'm going to allow my colleagues to jump in, okay?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So the block by block states that DCP and HPD will seek to use affordable housing fast track proactively, exploring city sponsored land use actions in these districts.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Is DCP currently studying conditions in the 12 affected community districts to identify opportunities for up zoning that will produce new construction affordable housing?

chapters.summary: He says they are assessing opportunities, the list was just produced, fast track goes into effect in January, and they will engage council members; no additional public analysis beyond methodology.
chapters.title: Chair Sherman says DCP is assessing fast-track districts, no public analysis yet

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So as noted earlier this month, we released the 12 affordable housing fast track communities.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: These are the communities where we've seen affordable housing production lagging.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We, along with our agency partners, are certainly assessing opportunities in those neighborhoods, whether we see opportunities for growth or well as opportunities for city-led housing initiatives, such as housing.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: that can be subsidized, as well as some of our Lyft initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so we're taking that look.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: The list was just produced earlier this month.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: The fast track goes into effect in January, and one of the things that we'd like to do is also ensure that we're in conversation with those members so that we can be strategic about the opportunities that are before us.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Will DCP be releasing any public analysis on the fast track?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So the analysis that we released really is the housing production level.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: As you know, and I know that we've had conversations with council members recently around the fast track, we have no specific plans at this time for actions in those neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We're literally assessing that as we speak.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And anything that we would move forward with, we want to make sure that we're having conversations with council members in those affected districts first.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so we've started some of that review.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I know I've had conversations with also coming out to certain districts to walk the communities, make sure that we understand what those opportunities are.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But there's no additional analysis other than the methodology that we use to determine the fast track neighborhood.

chapters.summary: He asks if the administration plans to connect with council members and community boards; Garodnick says they notified council members, reached out to all community boards, and have trainings and a public info session.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks about engagement with council members and community boards

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So the administration plans to connect with council members, as you state, that you already have been doing, and the community board while doing this fast track?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So when we announced the fast track, we also, as we gave notice to council members, we also reached out to every community board in the city, including those that were unaffected.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We have community board trainings happening right now, going through the fall, on a number of reforms, including the fast track.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And we also have a public information session in December to make sure that community boards, the public, are aware of the fast track.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I've also, as I've reached out to council members individually, have offered to also come out to do.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: and understand what the opportunities are there.

chapters.summary: He asks if DCP plans to partner with sister agencies to address development and upzoning; Garodnick says each neighborhood is different, and larger rezonings would come with investments.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks about partnering with DOT, schools, parks for infrastructure

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So with doing the rezoning in these specific districts, do you guys plan on partnering with sister agencies like DOT, New York City Public Schools, parks to address the development or the upzoning that you're trying to do in these communities?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So I would say that there's a question about scale, right?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So every fast-track neighborhood is different.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We have high-density districts, mid-density, low-density districts.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: The types of city-led actions that can happen in these districts also range.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Some offer opportunities for rezoning.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Some may be more appropriate for HPD affordable housing tools.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Some may be appropriate for some of the other city-led housing initiatives that we're looking to promote.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so I think we're looking at every neighborhood unique and in a unique way.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And any city-led action that we have would certainly happen in concert with conversations with council members, affected community members.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And where we, if we were to pursue larger scale rezonings, for instance, any of those neighborhoods, those would typically come paired with the types of investments that go with large scale rezonings.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But I would just note that many of the fast track neighborhoods are very unique, right?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So we have very, very, some very low density districts, as well as high density districts.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We really want to be thoughtful in the way that we're approaching those opportunities.

chapters.summary: He says members feel investment is not being talked about, focus is on upzoning and units, and asks how DCP can better communicate that they will prioritize full planning.
chapters.title: Chair Riley presses DCP on communicating infrastructure investment

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Glad to hear that.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I just feel like a lot of members feel like the investment aspect is not really being talked about a lot.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The focus is really on we need to upzone, we need units, and a lot of members have.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: specific concerns within those communities that need investment.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So what can DCP, I guess, do better with communicating that with members that you guys will be prioritizing, doing a full planning in those areas that you guys are focusing on, instead of just looking at just unit count and density and just upzoning?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So just to take a step back, capital planning is an exercise that happens across the city routinely, right?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: The vast majority of housing that's being developed in our city is happening as of right.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Neighborhoods are constantly changing.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: It's important that the city is constantly understanding its capital needs, status of good repair, and that's ongoing.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: As we start to pursue any city-led actions in these communities, we are also in conversation with our capital agencies to understand the infrastructure needs, planned investments,

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: as well as making sure that they understand these communities are prioritized for affordable housing as we start to assess those opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: If we were to pursue a larger scale rezoning, for instance, in one of those communities, we would certainly pair that with any investment that's needed to mitigate issues that may have emerged during our environmental impact study, the types of investments.

chapters.summary: Garodnick says typical neighborhood rezoning was 10,000-14,000 units, with examples like Bronx Metro North (7,000) and Atlantic Avenue (5,000), and investments aligned with growth.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks for definition of large-scale rezoning

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: What is a large scale?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Can you say for the record?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: What would that be considered?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: There's a range.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I mean, in the last administration, a typical neighborhood rezoning was anywhere from 10,000 to 14,000 new units of housing.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But we also have examples like Bronx Metro North, which was 7,000 units, right, along the corridor.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So, or Atlantic Avenue, which was around 5,000.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So there's a range depending on the study area.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But E.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Each of those projects came with investments that were aligned with the level of growth.

chapters.summary: Garodnick says yes, they welcome it, and mentions Councilmembers Santosuosso and Hanks looking at opportunities.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks if DCP will collaborate on council-led neighborhood rezonings

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The City's Council Planning and Land Use Division has begun working with council members in the fast-track areas to understand development potential.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: In some cases, council members and community boards may decide to propose ideas for neighborhood rezonance as a preferred way to add new development alongside community engagement and city investment in infrastructure and services.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Is DCP open to working collaboratively with council members and communities on this approach?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Yes, we welcome that.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And I know that Councilmember San Soso and a number of other council members have started to look at those types of opportunities, Councilmember Hanks, as well as opportunities in their community.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So we look forward to that.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We look forward to learning more details.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And we're happy to work proactively together.

chapters.summary: He asks if DCP will provide CPC capacity to engage on community benefits; Garodnick says yes, they ensure environmental review and mitigation, and CPC can recommend modifications.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks about CPC capacity and engagement for fast-track applications

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: In addition to potential DCP-led rezoning, is it...

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: It is also expected that the affordable housing fast track will lead to many private developer applications for which the city plan commission will now be the final vote.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: In the EULA process, tough issues are usually resolved by the city council's negotiation with the applicant on a final agreement.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: These agreements might include modifications and commitments for local investment or other community benefits.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: For fast-track applications, will DCP provide the City Plan Commission the capacity and resources to engage on these issues?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So when an application is moving through ULERP, long before it reaches the city planning,

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Commission at the department level, we also are ensuring to the extent that environmental impact review is required, we are ensuring that that's completed.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We're identifying whether there's a need for mitigation.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: The City Planning Commission has that information available as they start to research the proposal.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: There's certainly times in City Planning Commission hearings where we've brought up mitigation that has been identified in an EIS to ensure that the developer is committing to that.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: The City Planning Commission also has the ability to recommend modifications to the MIH options, for instance.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Typically, we have deferred to the City Council in those types of decisions, but when we are the final vote in some of the fast-track districts, those are the types of modifications we certainly can discuss and recommend and make as part of our final report.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I envision that we, in my role as department director in particular, that we remain in close conversation with the council.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And as you are well aware, a lot of the engagement around projects happens well before the formal public review process where developers are already engaging community council members and stakeholders

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: around priorities so that by the time they've reached the commission, there's been lots of modifications to applications usually before they get to the commission level.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So you still commit on engaging with council members through CPC within the commitments?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Sure, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And again, at the department level as well, too.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We certainly will ensure that we continue to engage with you all.

chapters.summary: He asks how DCP will be informed on open space, sewer capacity, school seats, etc., when projects skip environmental review; Garodnick explains the SEQRA exemption for modest projects and that land use review still applies.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks how DCP will assess infrastructure without environmental review

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: With the changes to SEEKER, many private applications will skip environments.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: With our environmental review, how would DCP be informed on whether there is sufficient open space, sewer capacity, school seats, pre-K availability, public transportation access, and other infrastructure to support development?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So there are a subset of projects now that are exempt from CCRA based on recent passage

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: at the state level, which really is exempting projects that are relatively modest, 250 units to low to mid-density districts, 500 in higher density districts.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: This exemption really came from a 10-year analysis that showed us that across all of these projects, less than 1% produce an environmental impact.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so these were projects that were previously really held in about two years of review where there was no impact produced, which obviously is adding time and cost.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Based on our analysis, we saw that it added over $80,000 in additional cost per unit.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so we will certainly continue to move those projects forward as they are seeker exempt, but they are still subject to land use review, right?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: That does not change.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: The ULERT process doesn't change either.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so questions about high density, bulk, all of the relation to the neighborhood, public realm, those questions will still come up and are part of our land use review process.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: What has changed, however, is the EAS process, which, again, based on 10 years of analysis, was not producing an impact or requiring mitigation.

chapters.summary: He notes the committee usually sees smaller projects, asks if DCP will still negotiate commitments; Garodnick says yes, projects outside fast-track still go to council, fast-track projects go through expedited process.
chapters.title: Chair Riley confirms commitments for larger projects despite SEQRA exemption

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: But on average,

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Chair, we don't really see those type of projects come to the committee.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: You don't really see the 250, 500 unit projects a lot.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: You really see smaller projects coming to the committee.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So just wanted to confirm that even though it is going through Seeker,

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: you are still going to have that same conversation with members to figure out what type of commitments.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: But these are technically kind of larger projects than we're used to seeing within the Land Use Committee.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And I will note that there are projects that are exempt from

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: SECRA, but are still subject to the traditional Euler process.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So if those projects are in districts outside of the 12 fast track districts, they are still going to the city council for final approval.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: The projects that are in the fast track districts would be the ones that are going through this expedited process.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: He notes DCP is only undertaking two neighborhood plans, asks if more are planned and if OMB set aside capital funding; Garodnick says they will continue neighborhood plans, and all plans are paired with significant investment.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks about pipeline of neighborhood plans and OMB funding

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Going to go into another set of questions.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So since 2016, neighborhood plan rezoners have been one of DCP's primary tools.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We're doing one in my district right now to add housing development capacity alongside infrastructure and community investment to support growth.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Over the last decade, neighborhood rezoners have enabled nearly 80,000 projected additional housing units.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: DCP is currently only undertaking two neighborhood plans, one in my district and one south of Prospect, as compared to the five neighborhood rezoners during the prior term.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Is DCP actively looking to add more neighborhood rezoners to the pipeline?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And does the administration have a goal as to the number of neighborhood rezoners it is seeking to accomplish?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And within that, has OMB set aside capital funding for those rezoners?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And again, thank you for your partnership on White Plains Road.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I know that there's been a lot of work that's going into that plan in particular.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So we announced our first two neighborhood plans early in this administration.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: They are the first two, but certainly not the last.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We will continue to move forward neighborhood plans.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We are also looking at other opportunities relative to the fast-track neighborhoods that may be more modest than our traditional neighborhood plans based on the scale of those communities.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But we know neighborhood plans are essential to really unlocking housing opportunity, but also ensuring that we're bringing economic investment, supporting job creation, making sure that we have livable neighborhoods that have been informed.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: By community input.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So there is a commitment to neighborhood planning, absolutely, in this administration.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And as we refine our plans, we would be excited to share more neighborhoods that we would like to focus on.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: With regard to your question regarding OMB investment and capital improvement, so all of our neighborhood plans, whether it's been the last administration or this administration, have been paired with significant investment.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And that is typically investment that emerges through, again, our environmental impact study, where we're identifying where there's a need for capital or other investment to mitigate issues or to, for instance, bring about new school seats.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: There's also a world in which we're looking to accelerate existing planned work based on the housing growth that we project, as well as investments tied to what we heard from community, whether it's street improvement or public realm, as well as services and opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so that will certainly be part of the White Plains Road plan, South of Prospect, and any other neighborhood plan that we move forward.

chapters.summary: He asks what a micro plan is and if it involves community engagement; Garodnick says it's a smaller planning approach, any city-led action includes engagement and investment, and they haven't identified specific plans yet.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks about micro plans and community engagement

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The Blah Blah Block report also proposes micro plans, a new concept of publicly led planning actions that are smaller than neighborhood rezoning.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: What exactly is a micro plan and would it involve community engagement and planning investments like a neighborhood rezoning?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So what we're really talking about is just a difference in planning approach.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Typically, as I mentioned earlier, we pursue large-scale neighborhood plans, which we will continue to do.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We have new tools at our disposal, such as eLERP, which is an X.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: expedited land use review process.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We have SECRA reform, which can allow the agency to potentially move in a way that's more flexible and more nimble for small-scale rezoning opportunities that may be a catalyst for a community that can help activate and unlock sites that can be suitable for housing.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Any city-led action will absolutely include engagement with communities and investment that's appropriate to the scale of the action.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: But what if there's multiple small projects in a single area?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: What does the approach DCPs want to take for that?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So we have not identified plans.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Right now we've been focused on larger plans.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I think as we get to a place where we're looking at smaller scale plans, we would certainly see what those plans mean in the aggregate and whether they are actually a larger plan.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But in all of those scenarios, we would still, again, identify opportunity for investment, make sure that we're engaging the local council member and the community.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Do you foresee the micro plans taking advantage of the secret exemptions?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So, yeah, and I would just, again, a plan is a plan regardless of the size.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: If we have a plan that is at the scale of secret exemption, that would allow us to move it along more quickly.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But, again, it doesn't change the land use review process.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We would still need to go through all the steps of ULERT.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: He says he will allow members three minutes for first round, starting with Chair Lewis, Chair Marte, then Council Member Sanchez.
chapters.title: Chair Riley pauses Q&A to allow colleagues to ask questions

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I'm going to pause there.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I'm just going to allow my colleagues to ask some questions.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So we're going to do rounds.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We're going to allow members to have three minutes for the first round, and then we'll go into a second round, okay?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We're going to begin first with Chair Lewis, followed by Chair Marte, then Perina Sanchez.

chapters.summary: She asks how DCP is planning for communities affected by the Interborough Express; Garodnick says TOD is a cornerstone, South of Prospect plan intersects with IBX, and they are planning long-term.
chapters.title: Council Member Louis asks about IBX and planning for central Brooklyn

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Riley, and it's good to see you, Chair Sherman.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Three quick questions.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: You mentioned in your testimony development of the Citywide Transit Oriented Development Initiative, and I wanted to ask you a question around Interborough Express.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Given that Interborough Express is still years away from operation, how is DCP planning for communities in central Brooklyn, including districts like mine, the 45th, that will be affected by the arrival of this new transit line?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you for your question, Councilmember, and thank you for your partnership on the South of Prospect plan.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Transit-oriented development is certainly a cornerstone of block-by-block.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: It offers a tremendous opportunity for us to focus on developing housing, developing affordable housing, and bringing New Yorkers closer to transit.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We have over 650 miles of transit in our city.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Believe it or not, some areas of our city, we still see outdated zoning, where the zoning is really not matching the potential that the transit offers.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So with respect to the IBX, one of our first neighborhood plans is South of Prospect, which we know will intersect with the future IBX line.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We have factored that into how we're planning in that community.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And by design, the IBX line, the nodes, right, connect to our existing transit system.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so there's a lot of opportunity for us to think about as we plan for growth around our existing transit system, how that also can set the stage.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: for future IBX as well as other lines.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: In the last administration, there was planning around the future stations of the Bronx Metro North.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And we know that the timeline for that has shifted, but planning is for the long term.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so, you know, we're looking at this work much, you know, very much in the long term and making sure that we're at least unlocking the zoning tools that we need to ensure that as those stations emerge, we've planned for the growth and neighborhood vitality that's needed, starting in South of Prospect.

chapters.summary: She asks if DCP has begun thinking about where housing would go around projected stations; Garodnick says they are in early stages, have had community engagement, and are hearing housing, street safety, and public space as priorities.
chapters.title: Council Member Louis asks about housing around future IBX stations

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Public engagement has begun on the South of Prospect neighborhood plan, thanks to your team, which is close to the IBX alignment.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: In the context of this plan, has DCP begun thinking about where housing would go around projected stations?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So we're still in the very early stages, particularly with...

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: In developing our overall transit-oriented development proposal, but also with South of Prospect.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So as you know, we had our kickoff meeting last month.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We had a really great turnout.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We've had over 1,000 residents participate in our survey.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We have some walk shops coming up this week as well, too.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so we've not yet started to project where housing will go, what potential zoning framework is in that district.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We want to make sure that we're hearing from community.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We certainly are hearing housing is a priority, street safety is a priority, public space is a priority.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so we're factoring all of that into the plans moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: She asks how DCP will approach private developers using the future IBX as rationale; Garodnick says they look at land use rationale, welcome transit-oriented development, but treat applications with same scrutiny.
chapters.title: Council Member Louis asks how DCP will handle private applications citing IBX

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: And how will DCP, and I think Chair Riley alluded to this earlier, but how will DCP approach private developers'applications?

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: who will use the future IBX as a rationale for their plans?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: That's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I think every time we receive a private application, we're looking at the land use rationale relative to the surrounding context.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We know that certainly locating housing

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: near transit is essential.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: It's a climate-friendly development.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: It supports fair housing.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so to the extent that applicants are looking to maximize transit opportunities, we certainly welcome that, right?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But we would obviously treat any application with the same scrutiny in respect to environmental review and land use review.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But those are certainly factors, right, where there's connectivity to transit is important.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Riley.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Marte.

chapters.summary: He says the block-by-block plan mentions 100 Gold but not the zoning text amendment allowing 30 FAR in Lower Manhattan, fears unprecedented development without proper discourse, and calls it a Trojan horse.
chapters.title: Council Member Marte raises concerns about 100 Gold and 30 FAR text amendment

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Thank you for being here, and thank you, Chair Riley, for hosting this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: In the block-by-block plan, 100 gold is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: However, what's not mentioned, a part of the plan, is the zoning tax amendment that's associated with the ULERP, which will allow 30 FAR in the whole special Lower Manhattan district.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: My fear is that you guys are allowing unprecedented development, and I'll give my colleagues here, most people don't even have R8 in their district, but a 30 FAR will allow,

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: like what's being proposed at 100 gold, which will allow 4,000 units in probably the biggest building in lower Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: And so allowing that to be mapped all throughout lower Manhattan with

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: having a proper discourse with other stakeholders in the community makes it seem like two things.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: One, you're using 100 gold as a Trojan horse to map the rest of the neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: And B,

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: there's not going to be an adequate discussion of infrastructure, school seats, or anything else because you're using it as a segmentation, right?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: You're trying to do one thing at a time so then it doesn't seem like a big proposal.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: And I know the response is going to say, well, the developers, whether it's the city or private, will still have to go individual rezoning because nothing is mapped.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: R12 in this community, but if you put the cart before the horse, then it might allow you to say, oh, there's not going to be an adverse damage to this community because you're going to be looking at as isolated individuals.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: And so, one, my recommendation is to separate that whole text amendment from 100 Gold.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: We can have that discussion and figure out a plan for that site.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: But what I fear is that you guys are actually not doing planning for my community.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: You're not thinking about the infrastructure for my community by going down this route.

chapters.summary: He acknowledges concerns, says lifting FAR cap creates new opportunities, 100 Gold is a tremendous opportunity for affordable housing, and they will follow up on the text amendment status.
chapters.title: Chair Sherman responds to concerns about 100 Gold and 30 FAR

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So I can jump in there and thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And I know I recognize your concerns.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Obviously, with the lifting of the FAR cap, it is certainly creating a new Manhattan skyline, a new city skyline, right, creating an opportunity to build in ways that we haven't before to really meet our housing crisis.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: There's a really tremendous opportunity at 100 Gold to create affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: in a neighborhood that, as you know, is very well connected to transit and other resources.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I think we certainly take your note regarding the text amendment and the actual action, both of which would require public review.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I don't have before me actually where the status of both of those.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I don't know if we have that, but we can certainly follow up with you on that.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But we want to make sure that as that project moves forward or any project, right, in a future RF,

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: 12, 30, any future district, particularly as we start to see these new districts emerge, that we're completing a study and we're understanding the community needs.

chapters.summary: He asks that the text amendment be a separate application; Edith Su Chen says any future 30 FAR application would require separate rezoning and notes a scoping hearing on October 29.
chapters.title: Council Member Marte asks to separate 30 FAR text amendment from 100 Gold

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: And I would ask that you just do it as a separate application.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: There's going to be a lot of stakeholders that aren't aware that you're even mapping a 30 FAR in their neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: And I feel like that's really disrespectful to our community.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I understand, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And my colleague, Edith Su Chen, also may be able to provide more detail.

utterances.speaker: Edith Su Chen
utterances.text: Yes, sure.

utterances.speaker: Edith Su Chen
utterances.text: Any future application of a 30 FAR would have to go through a separate rezoning before this body, before city council.

utterances.speaker: Edith Su Chen
utterances.text: And then with respect to where we are in the public process for 100 gold, a scoping hearing will be held on the 29th, October 29th, very soon.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: I completely understand that, but any future rezoning can be a spot rezoning, right?

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: It doesn't have to take that adverse impact that allowing a mapping of a whole district that even includes this.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: building and includes parts of the seaport parts of lower Fidei, I think is a way to get away from actually

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: thinking about what are some of the worst case scenario and how it's going to have adverse impact to our community, to our commercial businesses and to our infrastructure.

chapters.summary: She asks why long-term needs for deeply affordable and formerly homeless units were not included, whether demolition of rent-stabilized units was considered, how the 25% affordable target was set, and for a status update on Spotlight on the Bronx.
chapters.title: Council Member Sanchez asks about Fair Housing Growth Strategy and affordable need

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Next, we're going to hear from Councilmember Perina Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Riley.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And this is a moment where I appreciate that housing is split among so many committees because it's just so much to talk about.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So I'm going to ask all my questions in succession.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: First, thank you for meeting with us, the land use team, and our committee, taking some of our recommendations into consideration between the draft and final reports of the fair housing growth strategies.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Strategy, I was glad to see that access to transit and tidal flooding vulnerability have now been factored into the community district targets, but other factors specified in our local laws were not included.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Why did the administration not include specific long-term needs for affordable, deeply affordable, and formerly homeless units?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The draft and final plans speak only to the administration's commitments, but does not fully encompass the housing needs of New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And establishing the long-term need disaggregated by housing type is a clear requirement in local law.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Second, in some neighborhoods, channeling Councilmember Gail Brewer, generating new construction of affordable housing at scale may only be possible.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: possible with demolition of existing rent-stabilized units or other existing properties?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Has DCP and HPD considered this in setting new construction targets?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Third, how did the administration arrive at a citywide target of 25% affordable housing with only 7.3% at a deeply affordable level?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And finally, the block-by-block housing plan proposes a new planning initiative for HPD called the Spotlight on the Bronx,

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: an intensive planning process to coordinate proactive government actions in community districts 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, and 8, where HPD has financed tens of thousands of units of affordable housing, but planning for complete neighborhoods has lagged behind.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Can you provide us with a status update on whether the process has started?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: How are you planning to engage community boards and local elected officials?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And do you have specific areas of the Bronx where you are going to be addressing quality of life barriers like improved sanitation and public space?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And finally, is HPD going to be coordinating a package of capital improvements for these areas and engaging partner agencies?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Chair, I'm just going to ask, some people can't hear you online, so if you could just talk a little bit more into the mic.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Sure.

chapters.summary: He thanks the council for the Fair Housing Growth Strategy, says they are sensitive to displacement, and mentions state laws protecting rent-stabilized housing and tools like MIH.
chapters.title: Chair Sherman responds on fair housing and displacement concerns

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So thank you for your questions, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I'll kick things off and then I'll turn over to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I want to thank the council for your leadership in creating the fair housing growth strategy and requiring it.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: It really requires the city to be able to complete an assessment of the housing need that we have and really sets a goal for us to achieve.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: A lot of the work that we plan to accomplish through block by block starts to get us there, but with a commitment of building over 200,000 new affordable units and a number of the strategies that we've outlined in the plan sort of speak to that level of implementation.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Before I turn to my colleague to speak a little bit more about the methodology, I do want to address your question regarding rezonings and the potential for displacement.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: This is a very important question.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: As we are looking for opportunities for rezoning, we are certainly very sensitive to ensuring that we're not disrupting existing housing and particularly rent-stabilized housing and our deeply affordable housing that exists.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We know that there are a number of laws at the state level that make it very difficult to demolish, unilaterally demolish rent-stabilized housing in our city, in addition to tenant protections.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And a lot of the tenant protection work that's been happening in this administration has also been built to ensure that we're bolstering that.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so as we're looking at opportunities, particularly in neighborhoods that are dense, where we know development is happening, right, we're trying to find opportunities to use tools such as MIH to really pair affordable housing requirements with development activity that's happening.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: There's also opportunities for office to residential.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: as well as tools that the city has through its LIFT task force and other sort of subsidy tools that can be utilized in some of the development that's happening.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so ensuring that we are approaching our planning and our rezoning efforts with a clear eye towards tenant protection is important, and that's sort of certainly captured in the block-by-block plan.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: It's two very important strategies that go hand-in-hand.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I will turn it over to you, Michael, on the methodology.

chapters.summary: He describes the methodology using population data, difficulty predicting affordable need, and says the 25% target comes from the mayor's housing plan; 50% of financed housing is for extremely low and very low incomes.
chapters.title: Deputy Commissioner Sandler explains methodology for affordable housing targets

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: Sure, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: So just on the affordable need, I think the HPD and the DCP team really dug in on the methodology that was outlined in the legislation and tried to meet the letter and the spirit of this bill to create a citywide framework for how

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: What is the city's need in terms of creating housing and how should that need be distributed across the 59 community districts?

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: When projecting out in 10 years, we sought to have kind of methodological rigor and numbers that we could stand behind and that...

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: Felt like they were kind of defensible.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And so you'll see in the needs analysis, we use population data.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We looked at who is already here in our city that doesn't have housing and what type of housing is near, how much housing is needed to meet that need.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And then also what type of population growth are we expecting from births, deaths, in migration, out migration.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And in terms of looking at the affordable need, it's very difficult to predict affordable need given the incredibly constrained

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: environment that we have right now in New York City, we see that the city's, you know, the AMI, which is how, you know, affordable levels are determined in affordable housing in New York City is based around market rent.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And so eligibility for affordable housing is based around the city's fair market rent and who needs and who qualifies for affordable housing is very kind of circularly dependent on that.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: Availability of housing generally and what is housing costs in the open market.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And so we felt that it's very hard to know what the affordable housing need would be in 10 years if the broader housing growth has been met.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: It's very difficult to predict.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And so we felt that what was kind of

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: made the most sense to share with New Yorkers is what we're committed to do on affordable housing and that we know that there's a very incredible need right now and the mayor's block by block housing plan

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: has incredibly ambitious targets for affordable housing greater than we've ever done before and so we're sort of basing around like what what's

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: What's our North Star for affordable housing is based around those targets in the housing plan.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: On the, I guess, sticking with that for a second, your question about why was the citywide target for affordable housing 25%?

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: Again, that goes back to the affordable targets for the growth, for the...

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: Fair housing growth strategy come directly from the mayor's housing plan.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: So unlike the broader kind of overall housing growth projections, the affordable targets are what we're budgeting for and what we're planning for and what we want to hit.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: So those are the targets that come directly from the housing plan.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And the 25% is really a function of that's just what percent those targets are of that overall housing production that we're targeting for the city.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And then in terms of the deeply affordable target, again, those come from our budgeted projections through the housing plan.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We create affordable housing through a mix of as-of-right programs that have affordability levels that are set by those programs.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And then on the housing that we finance, 50% of that housing is for extremely low and very low incomes.

chapters.summary: He says they are kicking off the initiative, adding Community District 2, focusing on healthy homes, public spaces around affordable housing, and will start community board and council conversations later this year.
chapters.title: Deputy Commissioner Sandler provides update on Spotlight on the Bronx

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And then spotlight on the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We're very excited to be kicking this off and focusing on quality of life and health in the South Bronx and the Northwest Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: I'm happy to also note that we're going to add Community District 2 to that list of many community districts, which shares many of the characteristics of the other communities there.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We've started conversations with our interagency's partners.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We do see core partners at the Department of Health.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We're really focusing on healthy homes and how the housing stock in this community is impacting economic outcomes and health.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We're also working closely with the mayor's office to protect tenants, the mayor's office of community safety, and the New York City Housing Authority.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We started scoping out what this looks like, but really what we want to do is focus on not creating new units, but creating quality of life.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And so we're going to be focused on conditions inside of homes, combining enforcement and investments in healthy homes.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And then we're going to be focused on public spaces, especially focused around the public spaces.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: around existing affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
