utterances.text: We'll say that broadly, that's HPD supported affordable housing, NYCHA, or rent stabilized housing.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: There's large concentrations of this housing stock in these community districts, and what we hear from residents of these

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: buildings that we've supported through our programs is that the quality of life that they're receiving after moving into affordable housing is lagging.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And so we want to focus on public space maintenance, public space cleanliness, safety around affordable housing assets, and we'll be working with the various agencies, community partners, and landlords to achieve that and

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: want to start kicking off community board conversations, council member conversations, hopefully later this year.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: He says 4,000 units at 100 Gold is a spot zone, and the focus should be on comprehensive planning and investment in the total community.
chapters.title: Chair Riley adds to Marte's question on 100 Gold and comprehensive planning

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Going to go into Councilmember Carr, followed by Thomas Henry and Savina Brooks-Prowell.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Just one second, Councilmember Carr.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Just to add on to Chair Marte's question, I think what he's alluding to is how much is projected for 100 Gold Street?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Now, before 2021, I think besides Gowanus, we haven't achieved 4,000 units in a neighborhood plan.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And I think that's just, he's alluding to that's a spot zone and then wants to talk about a more comprehensive plan in the area.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And I think that kind of alludes to what we're trying to get at today is that the focus should not just be on the unit count within the area, but a more comprehensive plan in the area.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Because putting 4,000 people there and not making it.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: making sure that you're investing in the total community and listening to all stakeholders in the community is doing a tremendous disservice to New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So just wanted to pinpoint that, Chair, to you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Next, we're going to hear from Minority Leader Carr, followed by Thomas Henry and Savina Brooks-Powers, then Banks.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And we've been joined by Councilmember Lee.

chapters.summary: He expresses concern that the council no longer negotiates final details under ELARP, asks how DCP will assess infrastructure, who will handle it, and how local input will be incorporated.
chapters.title: Council Member Carr asks about ELARP, council role, and infrastructure assessment

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Riley, for hosting this very important hearing.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Madam Chair, thank you for being with us today.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I'm very concerned, and so are the many people I represent, with respect to the new approach under ELARP, where now the council no longer has a role in negotiating the final details of a plan, and it's...

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: You know, selectively applied, right?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And that was the intention of the revision.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And so now some members continue to have this role and others don't.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: In my own district, there's actually, you know, five community districts and three of them are going to be subject to the bottom 12 fast tracking and the other two aren't.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And so I'm just curious to know from your perspective with this new responsibility where you're going to be negotiating the final details of these projects as they come, what is going to be the approach to infrastructure?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: The chair was talking about this earlier.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: How are you going to make that assessment?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: You were asked earlier about, you know, what are you looking at in terms of these 12 community districts in terms of housing opportunities?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Alongside that, are you doing infrastructure studies to determine what is needed based on the expense?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: anticipated growth of the rezonings that you're going to be pursuing in conjunction with private parties.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Who are you going to be essentially giving this task to within the department?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Is it going to be the bar of directors?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Is it going to be held more centrally at the department with the commission?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Is it going to be certain commissioners who kind of take a more forward role in this?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Like we'd like to know what the structure is going to be as that happens.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And then how are you going to incorporate local input, whether that's from a member, a community board, members of the public?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Because I think the concern is that once this system is really put into effect, that any consultation is just going to be pro forma.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And I think that that would be, you know, again,

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: disservice was used earlier to be disservice to the communities represent if that turned out to be the case.

chapters.summary: He says projects will be treated the same, with environmental review, community board review, and public testimony; DCP has a stronger role in capital planning, and CPC can recommend modifications.
chapters.title: Chair Sherman responds to Carr on ELARP and infrastructure

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So, you know, I would note that we, as projects are potentially proposed in the fast track districts, we will treat them the same way we do projects today, where we are,

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: if an environmental review is, they are subject to one, right, we are ensuring that happens.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: If there's a need for mitigation, we're making sure that that's happening.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: There is still community board review, borough president review, as well as public testimony at the city planning commission.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: There's also department level work that happens during the pre-certification process as well, which leads to lots of proposal refinement.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And developers typically are refining proposals long before they reach the city planning commission.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: With respect to capital planning and capital needs, as I shared before, that really is an ongoing process, right?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: There is the overarching need for the city to ensure that we are strategically planning our capital resources.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: One priority that I've had since being in this role is ensuring that DCP has even a stronger role in the capital planning process so that we're aligning our resources along with where we see growth opportunity happening, and that's certainly in these fast-track districts.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But there's also capital investment that can be tied to certain city-led actions, larger-scale planning initiatives to the extent that those would be pursued in your district.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so I want to ensure you that as these projects move through, there is close attention to community feedback, to capital needs, to infrastructure needs, and certainly ongoing conversation with the council so that we can make sure we understand your priorities.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: The last point that I would flag is, as I shared earlier,

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: At the City Planning Commission, we do have the ability to certainly recommend modifications to applications before we approve them, such as changes to the MIH levels, for instance.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And typically, when we receive changes back at the City Planning Commission, right, for final scope approval from the City Council, we see those changes as well, too.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We often are not getting infrastructure changes back necessarily, but certainly changes around land use, affordability levels.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And those are all things that the City Planning Commission can consider as well, too.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so I want to assure you.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: you that we will give the time, the attention, and the thought that is necessary to ensure that these projects are a net benefit to the community.

chapters.summary: Carr says the council traditionally forced infrastructure commitments, and Garodnick notes DCP has borough teams, a centralized capital team, and climate/resiliency team.
chapters.title: Council Member Carr and Chair Sherman discuss DCP's role in capital planning

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I have to turn this back to the chair, but I would just say that you talked about the refinements that DCP and CPC already do in the Euler process, but typically speaking, what I'm talking about isn't part of that.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: It comes back to us to kind of add that to the tab because the administration of the day, whoever it may be, has not put that forward, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Members have forced the administration of the day to do that through the leverage that we've had in the Euler process, a leverage many of us will no longer have.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So I'm glad that you're kind of envisioning a greater role for CPC in the capital planning process because traditionally your role has just been you're really more of a department of zoning than a department of planning, respectfully.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So I just think, I just feel like there's no one in this process that will now have the tools to bring the investment that's needed to go along with the project.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Chair, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I would just add briefly, Councilmember Carr, you also asked where this sits in DCP.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So within DCP, we certainly have our borough teams who are excellent, right, and work with developers, partners, community groups every day around planning needs with across their boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We also do have a centralized team that's focused on capital.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We also have a centralized team that's focused on climate and resiliency that works across in coordination with our capital planning agencies.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so all of these agencies and departments will certainly have a role in how we consider these applications, as well as making sure the interagency coordination.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: is happening.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I hope you're proactive with this new responsibility.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I absolutely will be.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Mayor Lee.

chapters.summary: She asks if DCP can create a checklist for projects, whether homeownership will be considered, how many units are in the pipeline, and mentions Willits Point.
chapters.title: Council Member Thomas-Henry asks about checklist, homeownership, and pipeline

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Next, Councilmember Thomas Henry, followed by Brooks Powers.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: You have been very responsive and very effective in

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: to ideas, especially as it relates to projects in my area.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So I'm very thankful for that.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Kind of piggybacking off of the minority leaders, is there a way for you to put something, be it a checklist?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Again, going back to some of the things that we as council members on the floor identified during certain projects, I've had real world experience where no matter how many agencies you have look at something on paper, it's different when you're on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I've had land use experts come in and see a project that was zoned for one thing and get there and was like, oh my God, this cannot happen here.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So it's very different when you're live and in person.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And although you've been great, the next person after you may not be so amenable to the ideas of the council member.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So could there be a way for DCP to make as part of this process a checklist of things?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So even when we're looking at MIH, MIH in one and two don't necessarily fit the income requirements of my particular district.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And that's one of the things that we look at when we're reviewing ULERPs.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I'm going to do it all at once.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Homeownership opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I have a high homeowner population, one in single family homes as well as co-ops.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Will that be taken into consideration so that we're not just building more and more affordable units in these communities, but keeping...

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The continuity of community in place where you have long-term growth and opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And we're looking at 200,000 affordable units towards 700,000 units in the decade.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: How many units are currently approved in the pipeline?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So we're continuing to approve how many are in the pipeline.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: To be built against this 200,000 to 700,000 units.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And last but not least, if you're looking for opportunities, we have Willits Point, an additional 40 acres that are available for affordable housing.

chapters.summary: He appreciates the checklist recommendation, says they are looking at all tools including homeownership, and looks forward to discussions on Willits Point.
chapters.title: Chair Sherman responds on checklist, homeownership, and Willits Point

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember, and thank you for your partnership and many ideas as well that you shared, including Willits Point.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So to your first point, I appreciate that recommendation.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We'll certainly take it for consideration.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I want to make sure that we're listening to the council members.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We can think about a way to make that more routine or more systematized, but certainly appreciate that recommendation.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: With respect to homeownership, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So when we're talking about...

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: creating affordable housing opportunities in the fast track districts.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We're talking about everything, right?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Whether it's through zoning, whether it's through HPD affordable housing tools, which include in block by block and expansion of the city's affordable homeownership programs, as well as other opportunities that can be leveraged to facilitate affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so we're looking to deploy all those tools in ways that they make sense in those fast track districts.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so again, appreciate your insight and your recommendations around that.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And then to your last question, I know that there are ongoing conversations and efforts around Willis Points and certainly look forward to continuing those discussions.

chapters.summary: She asks how many approved projects are in the pipeline; Garodnick says he doesn't have the number offhand but will get it, noting most housing is as-of-right.
chapters.title: Council Member Thomas-Henry asks for pipeline numbers; Chair Sherman to follow up

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And do you guys know how many approved projects are in the pipeline?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So I don't have offhand everything that's in at least the DCP pipeline for approval.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We certainly can get that for you.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But I would just note that, as I shared earlier, the vast majority of housing that's being produced in the city is also happening as of right.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: There's housing that never comes before DCP or the commission.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And this is why the point that I raised around us also as a planning agency that also has a demography team, right, that's focused on New York City's growth overall,

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: working more closely with our capital agencies to anticipate needs, even for growth that is not necessarily being facilitated through zoning.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But we can certainly get that for you.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I know in our analysis of the fast-track neighborhoods, we certainly have what was produced in the last year.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We can share that and then give you a sense of what we understand right now from D.O.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: be permitted housing approvals.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: He mentions a tour of Willits Point, notes past projections of 5,000-6,000 units then 2,500, and encourages conversation with Thomas-Henry.
chapters.title: Chair Riley encourages DCP to engage with Council Member Thomas-Henry on Willits Point

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We're going to hear from Brooks Powers.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: But just to add on to what Councilmember Thomas Henry was saying about Willis Point, I did do a tour with her at Willis Point.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And I think in probably 2008, when this was first spoken about, I think they projected

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: roughly about 5,000 to 6,000 units of housing.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And then the last administration said about 2,500 units of housing.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: You have a council member here that will want to activate the other side of Willis Point, but it took us so many years to get to that point.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So I would just encourage, you know, having that conversation with Councilmember Thomas Henry because she is very adamant on addressing the housing need.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Revitalizing that area within her district.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Next, we'll hear from Councilmember Savina Brooks-Powers, followed by Banks and Carl Nassion, and then our majority whip.

chapters.summary: She notes Community District 13 will no longer come before council, asks how fast track will consider flood-prone communities, what say the community will have, and how surrounding neighborhoods' absorbed housing will be accounted for.
chapters.title: Council Member Brooks-Powers asks about flooding and fast track in Southeast Queens

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you, Chair Sherman, for, as my colleagues have said, your openness and willingness to communicate with this body.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I've had the opportunity to talk to you in advance of the recent announcement as well as

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: our more recent Zoom meeting, but I wanted to ask some questions on record just to have them here in a public space.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So starting in January, housing applications in Queens,

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Community District 13 will no longer come before this council.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Rosedale, Lawton, and Springfield Gardens are some of the lowest-lying parts of the city, surrounded by wetlands.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And residents are routinely faced with the threat of flooding.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: How will the fast track review consider these needs in a flood prone community?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And I know I mentioned this when we last spoke, but I just wanted to have it on the record in terms of response.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And what if it is found that the construction taken place creates additional flooding to neighboring homes?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: What say will the community at that point have?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And then also the fast track list is drawn on community district lines.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And Southeast Queens, as I often say, is made up of communities across multiple districts.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And together we built a significant amount of affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: housing when DCP plans city led actions in the 13th community district will it account for what the surrounding neighborhoods have already absorbed

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: even though it may fall in another community district so for example community district 14 did a significant amount but it it is a budding community district 13 and on the other side is community board 12

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: which just did the Jamaica

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: down up zoning in downtown Jamaica.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And so with all of that taken into place, it will just create an overwhelming increase in population in a community that has infrastructure resiliency issues and challenges.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: recognizing that the environmental review plan won't be the environmental review plan that we are accustomed to and that council members won't have as much of a say in terms of shaping it based on our local knowledge of the community.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: That's what the concern is.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So obviously I'm not opposed to development, but it has to be responsible in communities like this that have other underlying

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: issues that could impact what that looks like in terms of the health and well-being of the community.

chapters.summary: He acknowledges flooding issues, says they will work with DEP and capital agencies, notes the fast track is based on rate of production, and mentions the Jamaica neighborhood plan.
chapters.title: Chair Sherman responds on flooding and fast track methodology

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember, and thank you for raising these issues.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And I have familiarity with your district and particularly the flooding issues that you've shared.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so this is

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We are already well aware of this.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And again, it's a priority as we start to have conversations with DEP or other capital agencies about growth in these neighborhoods, right?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So that as we are leading any city-led actions, we're being attentive to the underlying infrastructure needs and the most appropriate places for that within your district.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I would also just note that the Affordable Housing Fast Track, again, was created through a rate of housing production, not a pure or raw number.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so...

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Production may look relatively modest in certain parts of your district relative to the overall rate that's being produced.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But, you know, it still may ultimately create a higher rate of production based on the housing dynamics in your neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so while

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: you know, this is a uniform methodology, it does account for the fact that every community is different and that's built into the way it was calculated.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so, again, I know that we'll be out to your district soon, but certainly want to take a nuanced look with you about where there could be opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And again, the types of tools, affordable housing tools, that make sense for that part of Queens.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We also recognize that at the end of the last administration, we completed a really large neighborhood plan in Jamaica.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We're really excited about that and excited to see the impact of that.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so there's a lot of opportunity already through that.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And we want to figure out how we pair that.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: with growth in other parts of your district.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And I will turn it over to my colleague at HPD.

chapters.summary: Sandler says new construction meets higher resiliency standards and retains stormwater; Brooks-Powers says past projects have shifted flooding problems, and asks about written responses and units waiting for financing.
chapters.title: Deputy Commissioner Sandler discusses resiliency standards; Brooks-Powers raises concerns

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, I just wanted to add that in many cases, new construction housing can be a positive contributor to neighborhood resiliency needs.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And new housing that gets constructed, it has to meet much higher standards for resiliency.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: It has to be built up above the city's flood elevation.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And then through the unified stormwater review, new housing construction typically comes with on-site retention of all stormwater that falls on that site.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And so in a lot of neighborhoods where you might have a surface parking lot, when it rains today, that water is flowing out into all of the neighboring sites.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And with new housing, that's an opportunity to retain that stormwater on site.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: So these are important conversations to think about how they work.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: Fit together.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But that has not been the case in some of the constructions, not only just housing, but just infrastructure, just new development.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So like we have a new Amazon facility has been there about four years now in Rosdale, where it did not flood before significant flooding.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But then there are other housing developments in the community and infrastructure projects that have happened even in Rockaway in the Arvin area that have pitched the streets wrong.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And while the infrastructure has been intended to, to your point, pull the stormwater and what have you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: To reduce what previously existed has created flooding in areas where it didn't exist before.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: So it's kind of shifted the problem now.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And in my last two questions before I run out of time, for DCP, barring our vote, will this commission respond in writing to the community board and council member recommendations on an application?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And for HPD, how many affordable units in Community District 13 were approved over the last five years but are still waiting on financing or construction start?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Because I'm wondering if it also counts or doesn't count towards this list.

chapters.summary: Garodnick says they will follow up on written responses to community boards; Sandler says many projects are waiting for financing and he will follow up on Community District 13 data.
chapters.title: Chair Sherman and Deputy Commissioner Sandler respond on written responses and financing

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Council member, you could come back for round two of questions.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Okay, I didn't know if the, I didn't hear the buzzer, so thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: But you can answer her questions right now.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So I certainly can follow back on, follow up on how we will follow up with community board, BP, city council recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Sometimes, in some ways, this is also codified in our CPC report, but we can follow up on that for sure.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And I think the second question was.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: Yeah, there are certainly a number of projects citywide that are waiting for financing.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We have more projects that we're working in our pipeline than we have resources to finance in any given year.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: Very excited about new resources that have been added to our budget through the housing plan.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And I don't have the data in front of me about Community District 13, but I'm happy to follow up.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: He asks what specific strategies are under consideration for NYCHA partnerships, including infill, land use, and transfer of development rights; Garodnick says NYCHA is pursuing opportunities, but no active proposal at this time.
chapters.title: Council Member Banks asks about NYCHA partnerships and infill development

utterances.text: Next, we hear from Banks, then in Carnation, then Hanks.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: housing opportunities and to generate revenue for public housing residents.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: However, the plan provides few details about how these goals will be achieved.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Can the administration clarify what specific strategies are under consideration?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Including infill development, utilization of NITRA land and the transfer of development rights, public-private partnerships, or any mechanisms that have not yet been disclosed to the council.

utterances.text: Sure, I can speak to this at a high level.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I know in the block-by-block plan, Mayor Mandani has made one of the most significant, I think the largest capital investment into NYCHA that we've seen from the city, which is really exciting.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And NYCHA obviously is continuing to pursue a number of development opportunities that are meant to bring capital dollars in to shore up their existing housing stock as well as contribute to our housing crisis.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: To the extent that NYCHA is pursuing transferable development rights, we stand ready to partner with NYCHA to achieve their goals.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: There's not an active proposal at this time.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We work very closely with NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Our housing team is in regular communication with the authority.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so as proposals or ideas move forward, we certainly stand ready to partner with them.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Well, specifically when it comes to infills, the city has previously pursued infill development on NYCHA-owned properties and other underutilized sites.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Candy administration.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: provide a breakdown of how many infield developments currently exist on NITRA property, how much revenue those developments have generated to date, and how those funds have been used to benefit NITRA residents.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: That's information we would certainly have to get back to you from NYCHA, and we're happy to follow up on that.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Typically, the actions that NYCHA pursues within their campus typically don't come before the CPC for approval, for instance.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so we can certainly make sure that we follow up with you, Councilmember, with the committee with those details.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And...

chapters.summary: He asks what criteria determine where additional density is allowed near transit and how residents can be assured of no overdevelopment; Garodnick says they are taking a citywide look, assessing all 600+ miles of transit, and will share a proposal.
chapters.title: Council Member Banks asks about criteria for transit-oriented development

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I want to cover a topic on transit-oriented development.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: The administration believes that transit-oriented development is a key component of the block-by-block housing plan.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What criteria is the administration using to determine where additional density should be allowed near transit?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And how can residents be assured that the transit-oriented development will not result in overdevelopment of outer borough neighborhoods or place a disproportionate burden on those communities?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Great question.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So we are taking really a citywide look at transit-oriented development.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: This is essential to how we grow as a city and also grow in a way that's climate-friendly.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: It also is essential to our fair housing goals to create more opportunity for New Yorkers to live near transit.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We are assessing the opportunity across our transit corridor, all 600 plus miles of it, relative to the zoning that currently exists along those corridors to really understand the potential

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: and look forward to sharing a more robust proposal.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But we're in the early days of that exploration.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We know in City of Yes, we created the qualifying residential areas, which allowed for really re-legalized, like some of the missing middle housing near transit.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so that was an approach to...

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: maximize transit in some of our low and mid-density districts.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so we're looking at a similar approach potentially in larger density areas, but we're still in the early days.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And we'll make sure to have conversations with the council as we start to move that forward.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you, Chia.

chapters.summary: She asks how the value of NYCHA land is determined, who determines it, and whether the city plays a role; Garodnick says DCP does not have a direct role, and NYCHA negotiates deals.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: Councilwoman Claude Narcion.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley

utterances.text: So there's not a role for DCP in that process.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But we can certainly coordinate with our colleagues at NYCHA and make sure to get a response.

chapters.summary: She expresses concerns about fast-paced construction quality, wage standards, and vacant privately-owned sites that have not been developed despite rezoning.
chapters.title: Council Member Encarnación raises concerns about building quality and warehousing

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And then I just have really two statements.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: One, I have some really serious concerns about the quality of the buildings and the developments that are happening at this fast pace.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: It seems like we're in a race to build fast and sometimes cheaply.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Often we're the ones here in the council that are fighting for wage standards, union standards, when we're looking at building and developments coming into our district.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And without those, we face, quite frankly, some developments that we're already receiving complaints from and brand new buildings, right?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Leaks, elevators that are not working.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: These are brand new developments that have come into the district and we're fielding real conversations with our constituents about the quality of the buildings that were built in this fast pace when they do not have all of these other standards attached to them.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So I just want to make a real plug for the fact that if our voices are out of that conversation when we're really fighting for those standards, that we have.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: a commitment from the administration that you will also be fighting for those wage standards and that union-built construction that will allow us to not have to feel those questions in the future.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And then, you know, warehousing is a big deal in my district.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: We went through an East Harlem rezoning to specifically try to make it more

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: attractive for developers to build that had been warehousing and sitting on developments for a really long time.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: We went through that rezoning.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: We utilized and threw everything in the book at them, and they still have not built.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: We are still sitting on those 10, 15 years later.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I mean, for some of those developments, my whole life.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And I'm just wondering if you had...

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Put any thought into how do we really incentivize these warehouse apartments that are just sitting vacant and in the face of people who are really in need of housing.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And that's all.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Garodnick offers to follow up on East Harlem rezoning and new zoning tools; Sandler says HPD has robust design standards and wage standards through the Construction Justice Act.
chapters.title: Chair Sherman and Deputy Commissioner Sandler respond on warehousing and building quality

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Just for clarification, are you speaking about vacant sites?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Vacant sites that are not HPD.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: They are privately owned, but we use the rezoning as a tool to incentivize that building.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: We said maybe if we let them go higher, it would help incentivize the building.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: That has not been the case.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And so we just, you know.

utterances.text: Outside of letting them build the Empire State Building in the district.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I don't really know what would incentivize them to build there, but something really does have to be done about the warehousing in the district.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I mean, they're just empty apartments sitting there, and it's quite...

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry

utterances.text: And I'm happy to also just have offline with you further about your district.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: There's always an opportunity for us to take another look at the right.

utterances.text: There are a number of new zoning tools available today.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: There are different types of affordable housing incentives that exist.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: There could be an opportunity for us to take a new look at what was achieved and what may need to be other strategies that we can use to make sure that we realize the goals of that plan.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So certainly happy to follow up with you on that.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And then I'll turn it to my colleague to speak a little bit more about development.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: Sure, and I'm definitely familiar with some of these Third Avenue buildings.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: I was involved in the East Harlem rezoning as well and remember a lot of these conversations.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And it's frustrating to hear that after all of these years, they're still sitting there on not filled.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: I think on the HPD side, we're definitely eager to find solutions to bring

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: if units are being held offline, to really understand why that's happening and find both enforcement tools and financial tools to kind of facilitate that to happen.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: So we'd be really happy to follow up on that.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: In terms of building quality and wage standards, for projects that are financed by the city, we have very robust design standards to ensure high quality housing.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And I think we've definitely heard about

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: kind of as a right development and lower quality that's there.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And so I think I hear you on that issue.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: I'd like to follow up and continue.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: discussing that.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: On wage standards, there are wage standards through the recently passed Construction Justice Act and sort of the projects that are being financed by HPD are coming with, I think, both that high quality that you want to see.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: She describes efforts to turn vacant sites into housing, asks how HPD and DCP can support, and what tools can expedite projects.
chapters.title: Council Member Hanks asks about North Shore planning and EDC partnership

utterances.text: Thank you, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: And committee staff, as I said before, we need to think about, you know, developing with a scalpel carefully, targeting developments with all our district needs.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: And you can hear that that's...

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Mainly what my colleagues are saying.

utterances.text: However, through the North Shore NYC, we're working to turn

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: vacant and underused sites into better housing, to better access our waterfront, and we want to understand the tools to expedite this process to build homes and our residents that can afford it and have the infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: To support them for generations.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So many of the projects in my district benefit from EDC stewardship, and I am really proud of that partnership we've implemented to advance the stalled projects and begin new ones.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: To this point, we've recently launched a community engagement and neighborhood planning effort to identify the next round of viable projects to continue growing

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: our pipeline for new housing.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: We want this pipeline to be, you know, executable.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: We want it to be real.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: How are HPD and DCP prepared to support these efforts, my efforts, and put a specific, you know, actions in place to move this, these plans forward?

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: I mean, I was going to ask the question about the pipeline and staying in the queue because we're now like a decade out on many of those projects that we were really proud to do last term or my predecessor did and we're just now doing these.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: So I think that's a really important.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: Part of, but it's been asked already and you answered it, so thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: But I do want to understand how we can work together, like what are the tools we need?

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: How could we expedite this?

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: You know, how do we get the eLERP process when we actually want to build and we have set up this, you know, this relationship with the city and the administration, city council is taking this big step forward.

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: And how are, what does that reciprocity look like?

utterances.speaker: Kamillah Hanks
utterances.text: How are we working together?

chapters.summary: He says DCP's Staten Island office met with her team, EDC is a partner, her district is not in fast track but tools like ELERP and SEQRA exemption are available.
chapters.title: Chair Sherman responds on North Shore and available tools

utterances.text: So thank you, Councilmember, and thank you for your leadership and really thinking through planning opportunities and growth opportunities along the North Shore of Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I know that our Staten Island office met with your team just this week, and we are excited to learn more about the planning effort that you have underway.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so to the extent that there are zoning tools or other tools that we can use to help realize the community vision, we stand ready to partner with you.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick

utterances.text: We've had some setbacks on the HPD project there, but I do think that we're in a place that we're hopefully going to be able to move forward soon.

utterances.text: And I think we want to do more work in Staten Island.

chapters.summary: She says she is not against development but sees no infrastructure plan, mentions flooding in Canarsie, and asks if DCP consulted DEP, DOB, or DOE before placing CB18 on fast track.
chapters.title: Council Member Narcisse asks about infrastructure and CB18 fast track designation

chapters.summary: He says the list was determined by charter-mandated methodology, and now the work begins to assess opportunities; he acknowledges capital planning is a priority.
chapters.title: Chair Sherman responds on fast track methodology and infrastructure

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So thank you for your question and also for sharing the concerns that you have in your district.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So the fast track list was determined really through a straightforward methodology that's consistent with what we're called to do in the charter.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So we are called to develop a methodology that determines a rate of affordable housing production and identify the communities that would be in the fast track.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We've done that.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We did that on October 1st.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And now the work begins, right, to begin to assess what the opportunities are in those districts relative to the existing conditions, relative to the need in all of the neighborhood contexts.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I know that capital planning and infrastructure has come up quite a bit in this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And trust me, I understand that that's a priority.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: It's one of my first priorities in this role.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: It's not as exciting necessarily as launching a new neighborhood plan, but it is critical to the work that we do at DCP if we're planning for a city that is growing and needs to continue to grow.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so as I've shared before, there are some new roles that DCP has in the capital planning process based on the last election where we have a role now to assess and score a certain city.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We also already have a role in the 10-year capital process.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We also have a role in working with community boards around their district need statements.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so we are ensuring that we're leveraging the roles that we have in the capital planning process to put growth at the front of it.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I don't want to take up your time.

chapters.summary: She asks about the 2080 flood plan, whether DEP, DOB, DOE were consulted, and how many affordable housing applications were proposed in CB18 in the last five years.
chapters.title: Council Member Narcisse asks about flood plan and affordable housing applications in CB18

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: In the 2080 flood plan, where we have homes that routinely flood after storms, and we are even sinking without asking DEP about sewers, DOB

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: about feasibility, or DOE about the school seat and everything else I include.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: That's one.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: In the last five years, how many affordable housing applications in CB18 did the council vote down?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And it's zero.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I can answer that, but you can continue answering it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So I want to know what's the problem.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How many affordable housing projects were proposed in CB18 in the last five years that HPD or private developers?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I think nothing has been filed because I want to know if it's because finances, if it was for the land desire, because we have not received any really.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So you can answer.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: He says he doesn't know the number of applications prior to his tenure, anticipates activity in fast-track districts, and says the list is based on charter methodology; Narcisse says it's one-size-fits-all.
chapters.title: Chair Sherman responds on CB18 applications and methodology

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Sure, I'll jump in.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So I don't know the number of applications prior to my tenure.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: can follow up with you on that.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I anticipate that there will be activity in those districts.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We're confident that there will be affordable housing development in all the fast track districts.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And again, we want to be sensitive to the needs.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I will just note that we have developed the list based on exactly what the charter is calling for us to do, developing a rate affordable housing production, producing the list without exception.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so that is the list as projects are pursued.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: That's where there's an opportunity for us to really assess the environmental impact, assess the infrastructure need, figure out the right mix and tools for affordability within your district, and customize the implementation.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But the affordable fast track list is developed strictly from the methodology that is defined by the charter.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: It is a list that accelerates the approval of affordable housing projects, the potential approval of affordable housing projects.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But it does not take away our responsibility to complete land use review.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So it's one size fits all, and it's not going to work, and it's not a blanket for all New York City.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Like I said, we build on marshland, and I love, appreciate you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm looking forward to see what spot that we can build.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And if not, we have to be sensitive to folks because they cannot even pay to repair their basements.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

chapters.summary: She says affordable housing at 80% AMI costs more than market rate in her district, asks how DCP deals with this, and says building more affordable housing drives market rate up.
chapters.title: Council Member Zhuang asks about AMI vs market rate in her district

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Councilmember Zwing, followed by Brewer, Santus, Woso, and Lee.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And also thank you for coming here today.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And I give you some background in my district.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I have Community Board 11.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: cost of one bedroom for two people in my district is lower than $2,400, but while affordable housing for two people couple at 80% AMI costs

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: $2,430, actually it's higher than our market rate.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So for this type of situation,

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We need to build more affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Yes, I agree we need to build more affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: That actually drives my market rate up.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: People not able to afford.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We are not Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Our rent originally not that high because we need to build more market rate.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: More affordable housing, our rate actually drive up.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: How do you deal with this type of issue?

chapters.summary: He says MIH levels are based on AMI, sometimes close to market, but MIH rents do not accelerate like private market, and HPD has other tools.
chapters.title: Chair Sherman responds on AMI and MIH levels

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Yeah, so we are defining affordable with MIH levels as the floor and any other types of affordable tools, right, that are above that, meeting the requirements.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so we know that in certain parts of the city, because the MIH levels are developed based on the AMI, right, certain parts of the city, it's close to what you may see in the market for existing housing stock.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But it's still often we see as more affordable than what may exist in brand new construction.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And what's important to note is that when we've been able to include mandatory inclusionary housing in projects, we know that the cost

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: of that housing, the rent will certainly not accelerate over time the way rent in the private market does.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so these are all, it's a very certainly careful analysis and calibration to how we would approach this in different districts.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I would note that that certainly is in reference to the affordable tools that are created through the MIH program, but there are other tools as well to create affordable housing that our colleagues utilize at HPD.

chapters.summary: She asks why ELERP doesn't account for population density, and why no Bronx districts were selected for fast track despite having more housing units than her district.
chapters.title: Council Member Zhuang asks about density and Bronx fast-track districts

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Why doesn't Euler's action process take into account population density?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Higher density district has less open space available to use, so the burden on them is higher.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So the Euler process does take into account existing context, land use rationale, as well as to the extent that a project is subject to environmental review, it does certainly take into account open space.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And typically in our high-density districts, we would see that because people are building much bigger projects.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so all of that is certainly factored into how we would make planning and land use decisions.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And the zero district in Bronx, sorry, was selected for Euler.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Are we...

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Are we to believe there's no district in entire borough needs more affordable housing?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: No, actually no one of the districts in the Bronx has more housing units than our Brooklyn CB11.

chapters.summary: Garodnick says every neighborhood is appropriate for affordable housing, fast track targets lagging production; Sandler explains AMI is based on market rents and HPD ensures highest AMI tier is below market.
chapters.title: Chair Sherman and Deputy Commissioner Sandler respond on density and AMI

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So we recognize every neighborhood in New York State.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: is an appropriate neighborhood for affordable housing, right, and can benefit from affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: The neighborhoods that are in the fast track are the neighborhoods where we have seen the production of affordable housing lagging.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And the goal is to be able to fast track affordable housing in those communities.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: It still does not take our focus away from building, facilitating, supporting the creation of affordable housing in community districts citywide,

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: including the Bronx, which we see is leading the city in affordable housing production, but where we still are promoting and advancing affordable housing projects in the borough.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And I'll turn it over to HPD.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: I just wanted to respond to your first question about AMI and its relationship to market rents.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: AMI in New York City is very high.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: The area median income name is actually a bit of a misnomer, and in New York City it's based around market rents.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And so because market rents keep going up in New York City, AMI has gone up every year quite significantly.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: So there are many parts of the city, including your district, it sounds like, where 100% of AMI is above market.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And HPD does not finance affordable housing that is above market.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: So in all of our projects that we're financing, we work to ensure that the highest AMI tier in our project is at least 20% below market.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: So for projects that we get financed in a neighborhood where AMI is lower than market, we're making sure that the highest AMI tier is maybe 60% of AMI instead of 80% AMI in those neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And for projects that are utilizing our as-of-right tools, we also include...

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: encourage them to have the highest AMI tier be below market because if the highest AMI tier in a project is at market or above market, those units are not going to fill.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And they're going to sit vacant on Housing Connect, and that's going to be bad for sort of everyone involved.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Zwing.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Just want to indicate the Bronx has been doing their fair share in the affordability crisis.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: That's why we were in that list.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: But as you said, Chair, every district in New York City can't do their role with producing more affordable housing units.

chapters.summary: He notes the Bronx has done its fair share, mentions AMI mixing with Westchester, and asks if there is energy to address AMI; Sandler says he can't speak to mayor's conversations but HPD serves right incomes.
chapters.title: Chair Riley raises AMI issue and conversations with federal government

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I'm going to go and...

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I wanted to touch really quick on that AMI issue.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We do even see places like in the Bronx where the AMI is being mixed with, you know, parts of Westchester.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I know the mayor has been having several conversations with the president and just wanted to know if there are any energy with addressing that AMI issue that a lot of people in the city are seeing.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: Well, I certainly can't speak to the mayor's conversations with the president.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: I can't say on the topic of AMI.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: I think that really the most AMI is it's all relative, right?

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: So I think the most important thing is that the projects that we're creating are serving the right incomes.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And so when we're looking to finance affordable housing, you know, our goal is.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And what we're committed to in the housing plan is that 50% of the housing we finance will be for extremely low and very low incomes.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And we're always open to...

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: having conversations about what are the right incomes for each project that we should be serving.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: The deeper affordability, the more subsidy, but we're committed to providing deep affordability in our projects.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And again, to want to be providing affordable housing that's above market.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: That's not the goal here.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I think some more conversation needs to happen around that.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We're partnering with everyone in government, local, state, and federal.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: That conversation can happen all day.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So I'll move on to Councilmember Brewer, followed by Satu Suoso, then Lee.

chapters.summary: She says the Upper West Side wants affordable housing but has no vacant land, asks why it's on the list, and says conversions of SROs are not counted.
chapters.title: Council Member Brewer expresses frustration about Upper West Side on fast track

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, you can imagine I am really pissed, and I find that this conversation is...

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Councilman Bill, can you just speak into the mic a little bit more?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: This thing doesn't...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I can't move it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: No, it doesn't move.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So my question is, in the Upper West Side, we want affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We always have.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But you don't count conversions of SROs, which is what's happening now, because that's not an immediate from bottom up.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Also, I want to pick up on the chair.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I've done over 200 ULERPs, more than anybody else.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I will say, I always say in Manhattan, we'd like to have some affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And he said, no, no, no, Gail, we're going to the Bronx because the land is cheaper.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So screw you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You're not getting affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You're not getting vouchers.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We're just going to do market and then hopefully some MI8.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I don't understand why is the Upper West Side on this list when there is not one vacant lot available?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How can it be on the list if it's not possible to conform?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Can you answer that question?

chapters.summary: He says the list is based on charter methodology applied without exception, notes development is happening on Upper West Side, and mentions MIH and HPD tools.
chapters.title: Chair Sherman responds to Brewer on fast track methodology

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So, Councilmember, thank you for, and I know your frustration.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I am beyond pissed.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: As I noted before.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We developed a list based on a methodology that's consistent with the charter.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: It is applied without exception across all community districts.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So how are you going to implement on the west side when there's no land?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So I will note that development is happening on the Upper West Side.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Give me an example.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: There are development projects happening on that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Yeah, and Edith is not helping us with the ABC land.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You want 2.4 acres, no help from HPD or the city to get it to be affordable at a reasonable rent, and he wants to build bigger than the entire state building.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So, again, I just want to note that...

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Where development is happening, there are tools that we can use like mapping, mandatory inclusionary housing, so that new development activity is subject to a requirement for affordability.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We can also, again, explore where the HPD financing tools, for instance, could potentially be utilized.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I've heard it all before and I never get any help.

chapters.summary: She says she will vote against ballot initiatives, asks how the city will get 12,000 units, and says the only way to change it is to go to court; Garodnick says they are focused on implementation.
chapters.title: Council Member Brewer challenges Chair Sherman on Upper West Side targets

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm just telling you, you haven't been around that long and I have.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I recognize that.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And I recognize your commitment to your district and commitment to affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We have an opportunity now to figure out how we fast track affordable housing together.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, I understand that in what we're going to vote on November 3rd, I'm voting against all of them, just so you know.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But understand that the 7% is even an increased amount of projected wanted housing on the Upper West Side.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How the hell are you going to get what you had before?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, they were voting on the ballot initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I hate them, just so you know.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And so the question is, understanding that in that ballot, there will be a projected even more required housing on the Upper West Side than there was in the past.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You're trying to get 12,000 units or some crazy amount out of the Upper West Side.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Where are you going to get that?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So with respect to the affordable housing fast track voted in the last election, there is not a numeric target that's required, right?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
