utterances.text: Yeah, but whatever's on the bottom 12 is where it ends up.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But we've created a rate, and the rate is relative to your overall housing production.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We have housing production.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You just don't count it because it's conversion and not new.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have three conversions, and you don't count them because they're not new.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So it does have to be new affordable housing units.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so it is a rate, though, so there's not a raw number.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: There's a way in which in the next five-year calculation, the Upper West Side may look very different based on the rate.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I don't care about five years.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I only care about now.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Okay, well, the next five years is when the calculation would happen again.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So the only way to change it is to go to court.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The only way to change this is to go to court.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So we're focused on implementation.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm focused on changing it and going to court.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I almost did not want to stop Councilmember Bruick.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I was scared.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: She's extremely, extremely frustrated at this process.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So thank you, Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Councilmember Santus-Wosso, followed by Councilmember Lee.

chapters.summary: She says Bay Ridge rents are relatively affordable, MIH apartments are more expensive than average, and asks what DCP will do to ensure deeper affordability now that council loses negotiating power.
chapters.title: Council Member Santosuosso asks about MIH affordability and loss of council power

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And as someone who is...

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And as someone who is also on the list and also frustrated, I nonetheless appreciate the ongoing conversation with your office.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And thank you for acknowledging our efforts around the Bay Ridge Triangle rezoning.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I think one of the reasons I'm frustrated is because, sort of as Councilmember Zhuang was saying,

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Relative to the rest of the city, Bay Ridge rents are relatively affordable, which includes a lot of rent-stabilized units.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And so while I still have Euler power, I've approved 400 units on my old block alone.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Both the market rates and the MIH apartments in both of those buildings are more expensive than the average Bay Ridge rent, which includes rent-stabilized units.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And notably as they passed through city planning review I did not see city planning specifically argue for a deeper level of affordability

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: and so I'm just concerned that if there is now that I can no longer use my power as a council member to negotiate for deeper affordability I'm concerned that that need will not be acknowledged or pushed seriously through

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: through the city planning review so I guess my question is now that we're losing this power, what will you do to make sure that the...

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: rents that are coming in are not merely inflationary to existing Bay Ridge residents while it purports to solve an affordability crisis elsewhere.

chapters.summary: He acknowledges tension, says CPC can modify MIH levels, and proactive planning can lay out tools for deeper affordability; East New York example shows mix of MIH and city tools.
chapters.title: Chair Sherman responds on MIH affordability and deeper affordability tools

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And again, thank you for your efforts and planning work that's happening in Bay Ridge.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I recognize that in certain parts of the city, there is that tension based on the AMI and the MIH rent calculations where the affordable rents are very much in line or sometimes a little bit higher than what we're seeing in the existing housing stock.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We are seeing, though, that the MIH rents are still comparable to what would be new housing that's built or sometimes much more affordable, and they also carry that permanent affordability.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: That being said, as I noted, at the commission, we certainly have the ability to make modifications and recommendations around the MIH levels that are selected.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I think also in your proactive planning process, I think that's also where there's an opportunity to lay out the intentions, but also the tools that may need to be at the table outside of MIH to get the deeper affordability.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And that was my next question was, is there a tool available in the arsenal if my proactive planning effort were to be successful where we could essentially...

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: You know, through the rezoning, strongly advise or force a deeper level of affordability.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that there's, I think there's opportunity for that.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: There's also, again, and I would defer to my colleague at HPD, other housing financing tools, right, that can be utilized.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I think the East New York example was shared earlier today, where we've achieved over 6,000 units, but really, really deep affordability.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: That's a combination of MIH, but also city.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: affordable housing tools, right?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: There's a mix.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so I think taking this proactive approach is helpful so that we could figure out the right mix in your community.

chapters.summary: She asks what capital investments are planned for TOD, especially with the R train, and if there's a role for council; Garodnick says they are in early conversations with MTA and welcome partnership.
chapters.title: Council Member Santosuosso asks about transit-oriented development and R train investments

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And then my last question is around sort of transit-oriented development.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: One of the reasons I'm trying to pursue the triangle rezoning is because it's so perfectly situated between two

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: to train stops, right?

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: 86Th Street and 95th Street.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: The trouble is that if you've ever taken the R train before, you will never want to take the R train again.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And so my thinking is, you know, it's one thing to talk about capital planning as far as city infrastructure that we fund and that we have control over.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: But it's quite another to talk about largely state-funded capital improvements, which in this case would be the R train and everything that it would take to get it to be a train that is a dignified option for everybody in southern Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: So what capital...

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Investments and planning are you thinking about specifically in transit oriented developments particularly if we're thinking about adding thousands of new residents within one to two train stops and thank you for your time thank you for that question so as we are

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: assessing and sort of developing a citywide transit oriented development proposal we've also have started early conversations with the mta as well to understand i know that they just released their capital plan a plan to bring

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: mta assets to a grade of and mta assets to a state of good repair which is really exciting.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so we are in those conversations to also figure out where there's alignment between housing.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: growth and investment.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We have tools like zoning for accessibility as well too, although I know the 86th Street station is accessible, which is great.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And some of the other, exactly, I know your district very well and also that you have accessible stations, which is really fantastic.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But we also are looking at other ways that we can utilize that program to support other types of infrastructure investment in transit that is as substantive and critical to what riders experience.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And I would just say if there's a role for the council to play or those of us in the bottom 12 to play where we are advocating with our state partners to get some kind of coordinated focus on these transit-oriented areas and developments, then I would love to play a part in that.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And we welcome your partnership.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And, again, we're still in early days, but we look forward to those conversations.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

chapters.summary: She describes her district's infrastructure challenges, asks what standards will evaluate sewer capacity, drainage, transportation, and who will ensure commitments are met; she cites Creedmoor as a successful community input example.
chapters.title: Council Member Lee asks about infrastructure standards and community input

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Council Member Lee?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: All right, so now moving over to Eastern Queens.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I'm almost visualizing hearing everyone's questions, what their districts are like, but I have a very interesting and challenging district in the sense that I think we're only one of two that has no subways and no railroads within my district.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: We're like, it's outside, north and south, but, you know, so when folks say, hey, we'll come meet you in your district office, I'm like, I think you might want to rethink that one, but, because it is quite far.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so it's interesting.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I just want to emphasize, I know I sound like a broken record at this point when I talk about infrastructure, but, you know, I have parts of my district.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I have four community districts, actually.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I have 8, 11, 12, and 13 in my council district.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so myself, you know, Deputy Speaker Williams, as well as Sylvina Brooks-Powers, we share CB13.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And there have been some significant infrastructure challenges there.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: One thing I will say is that, you know, for CB12,

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: That's where Hollis is.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: That's where the flooding happened, where, as you know, we recently had to vacate two homes because one of them was literally falling off its foundation from all the flooding damage and had to be demolished, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so there are really significant challenges where, and the city, by the way, put in $20 million underneath the ground.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: To sort of help with the water, and it did nothing to alleviate the flooding that's happening.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So in all honesty, it probably would have been better in a buyout program, but that's just, you know, I think what some of the residents have been asking about.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: But, you know, when it comes to infrastructure, I guess I'm just wondering, and I'll ask my questions first and go through it.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: What standards, I know a lot of folks have been asking, but what specific standards or metrics are you going to use to evaluate sewer capacity, drainage, transportation, and other needs?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And what happens if those systems cannot support the proposed housing.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So that's the first part of my question.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And then sort of piggybacking off Councilmember Santos-Oso with the community input piece and now that being taken away.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: When it comes to accountability, who will secure and follow through on infrastructure and community commitments, and how will residents

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: know whether those commitments are being met.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Like, how is that going to actually play out?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And also, lastly, I just want to really emphasize the community input piece of it, because Creedmoor, you know, if you look at my district, I think it's about over 90% is homeownership, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And the question I've always been asking is, we're not against building housing, but number one, it has to make sense.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And number two, it has to be in places where, you know, like we don't have that much land available because it's either parks or one or two family homes.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I rarely have any zoning that's above R3 in my district, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I think the place that could be looked at are the corridors where you could maybe build some units on top, but then there are challenges there because it's literally block and lot versus looking at how do we change maybe some of those areas.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: But, you know, the community input piece, when it came to Creedmoor, we got the community there with the civics.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: The community boards, our borough president, state senate, you know, assembly, as well as myself, because the Creedmoor, we successfully got the community on board with 50 acres.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So there's more than 50 acres.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: That is one place that's state-owned, so I know it's not city.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: That project is going to bring about 2,000 units as well as veterans housing, senior affordable housing, a school, firehouse, all of those things, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And that was done and was so successful because of the community input.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so I just lastly wanted to ensure how, you know, we're going to make sure that their voices are still part of that process, because I do ultimately think that will lead to a successful project.

chapters.summary: He says capital investment will be front and center, public engagement will continue, and they will get back to her on metrics; projects in flight will be part of next analysis.
chapters.title: Chair Sherman responds on infrastructure metrics and community engagement

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And thank you for sharing the Creedmoor example.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So we've heard loud and clear today, certainly, that capital investment and understanding capital needs is critical.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And that will be front and center in the way that we approach all of our work, but certainly the ways in which we assess opportunities within these affordable housing fast track districts.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Public engagement as well will be critical.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I would just note that the fast track does not remove community board review, borough president review, public hearings.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Those processes are still in place and part of our ULIP process.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And any engagement that happens pre-certification, including engagement with council members, and a lot of that happens informally, that that would still continue.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And we would certainly encourage that as those projects start to move into public review.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: In terms of metrics, I think we can get back to you with that.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: There are certainly certain measures of analysis that are part of environmental impact studies that we would use to have assessment.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: There's also the metrics that our capital agencies use overall to understand state of good repair and capacity.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so I wouldn't want to give that to you just offhand, but we can certainly share that with you.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And I don't know if there were any additional questions that I may have missed.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: The one thing I would note is that affordable housing projects that are in flight, like some of the work that you.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: you've mentioned, those will be part of the calculation in the next time we refresh this analysis and this methodology.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so we know that there are affordable housing projects that may be permitted during this period and start to move forward, which also may change the rate across the affordable housing fast track neighborhoods as we go into the next five year cycle.

chapters.summary: She asks if DCP factors in history of bad landlords; Garodnick says CPC reviews zoning appropriateness, and HPD takes enforcement seriously with programs like Fix the City.
chapters.title: Council Member Lee asks about bad landlords proposing projects

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Okay, sorry, Chair, I just have one last question, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And do you guys factor in, when you're looking at the proposals that you get, if there's history of bad landlords that are proposing these projects?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Because I actually have examples of that in my district, where there are proposals being made, but the folks that are proposing it,

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: haven't been good landlords with what they have now, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so I don't necessarily want to be in a position to say, yes, we need housing, but I don't want to reward bad behavior as well.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so what are some of the stopgap measures that are there in terms of how we can, you know, prevent that?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So typically at the City Planning Commission, when we're reviewing an application, we are primarily making sure that the underlying zoning is appropriate for the community.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Should the owner, landlord, anybody change over time, for instance, right?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We need to make sure that it's a solid rationale for the community.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: That being said, we certainly have testimony from the public and are able to ensure that we're asking questions when it comes to who the potential operators are.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But we also recognize that sometimes operators change over time.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so what's most important is making sure that the underlying.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: zoning makes sense for that neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: That being said, there are certainly other tools in the city to ensure that landlords are good actors, as well as taking action against those landlords who are not.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so I'll certainly turn it to my colleagues at HPD to speak to that.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that we take enforcement of tenants'rights and tenant conditions really seriously, and I think we're rolling out a lot of new programs in this administration.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: I think my commissioner, Commissioner Levy, talks about putting bad landlords out of business, and I think she's serious when she says that.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And we're recently launching the Fix the City initiative, which is really supposed to tackle these longstanding bad landlords,

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: recognizing there are good landlords out there, that not all landlords are bad actors, but for those that are bad actors, we do want to enforce against them.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And if there are folks in your community that we should know about, we should connect.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Actually, Commissioner Levy was very helpful, and she knew exactly who I was talking about when I brought her up.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: She knows all of them.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

chapters.summary: He asks if there's a deadline for the TOD plan; Garodnick says they are in early stages and hope to start conversations with council early next year.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks about timeline for transit-oriented development plan

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And just kind of piggybacking off the TLDs, is there a specific deadline that we can anticipate now that we'll see that plan?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you for your question.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So we are in the early stages.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We hope to, you know, early next year start to have conversations with the council about our approach.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But we're still in the very early days of that planning.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And I just kind of the same thing as Council Member Sanchez also is saying, like the community-based train control.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The issue that we're seeing in my district, I know like on the weekends, the five train is extremely spotty.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So we might be considered as a vibrant TOD district, but the people that live there on a day-to-day, similar to what Councilman Thomas Henry stated, since I've been living in that district, every single weekend it's been a challenge with the five trains.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So just wanted to kind of understand the metrics behind the TOD design and for you to have that at your mind when you are completing this project or when you're going to be posing that to the council.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: He asks how DCP influences capital improvements given no capital budget; Garodnick says DCP coordinates and has a role in 10-year capital plan, but is not an implementation agency; Chair Riley pushes for more influence.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks about DCP's role in capital planning and infrastructure investment

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Can you expand on what DCP role is in the capital planning process, given that the department does not have their own capital budget?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I know you spoke about different partners with DOT, Parks Department, but it kind of felt like you was kind of pushing the capital projects on those other agencies.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Is there any planning with DCP with those agencies as you're developing this plan?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So when we complete neighborhood plans, for instance, and there are a suite of capital commitments and other infrastructure commitments, those agencies who are the experts who are in charge of implementation lead and fund that work.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: DCP has a role, though, in coordinating and making sure that those projects are moving forward, particularly if they're connected to a neighborhood plan and publicly reporting that and making sure that that's happening.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Big picture, DCP has a role in our city's overall 10-year capital planning process, and I know we're going into an upcoming.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And as we do that, we are factoring in all the things that are new, right?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We have a fair housing growth strategy.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We have neighborhood plans underway.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We have new tools in priority neighborhoods through the fast track.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so we're bringing all of that into our upcoming planning process so that we can really ensure that our agencies who are planning for climate and resiliency and infrastructure needs are also attuned to where we see the potential for growth.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: The other note that I would add is...

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: What makes the 10-year plan relevant to DCP?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So it's relevant, and DCP has duties outlined in the charter with respect to the 10-year plan because we are the agency that's planning for the future, right?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We should be able to...

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So shouldn't your role in capital investments be a little bit more than letting that go to the sister agencies, being that you guys are in charge and playing the future?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I mean, I think that our role is really being able to plan for the future, plan for growth in the future, but not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I don't see DCP as an implementation agency and implementing complex capital projects necessarily.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We do also have a role now, based on the last ballot measures, of also assessing some of the city's capital assets and city facilities and making that information publicly available.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So we've been taking that on.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: But, you know, our role as a planning agency is to really make sure that whether it's through zoning, through our demographic work, really that we understand and help plan the future of the city and that we're ensuring the many agencies that play a role, whether it's.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: developing school seats, whether it's dealing with our sewers and our infrastructure, parks planning, et cetera, that those agencies are armed with that information and that approach so that we're planning in concert.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: The last thing I would also add is that we obviously also have a role in working with community boards and their district need statements.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And, you know, we want to make sure that as we go into our upcoming planning process that the priorities that are coming from our community boards are also factored into how we're considering city investment.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I just want to emphasize, I hear you, Chair, and I thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I just feel like, you know, being that we're planning specific neighborhoods and we're developing, I just think the role of DCP when it comes to infrastructure investment, I think within a lot of the members here today, you didn't hear that there was a hesitance of them actually wanting

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: development in their district.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: It was just the planning aspect of the infrastructure, the investment in certain communities.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And I don't want to beat that drum, but that's what you're going to hear, because a lot of these communities, it's a tremendous disservice to add people to a community that hasn't had that investment.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So just thinking about, you know, the structure of how DCP has any influence on those capital improvements, I just think you guys need a little bit more influence on that when we're talking about comprehensive planning in communities.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We're in alignment, for sure.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And I will say, as I mentioned earlier, coming into this role, that was certainly one of my first priorities.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We do have a centralized team that coordinates across the capital agencies.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so we're making sure that we're taking a stronger role in that process.

chapters.summary: He notes DCP added 41 new staff in FY27 budget, asks if any for neighborhood planning; Garodnick says 46 new lines for new responsibilities, including SEQRA-exempt applications, census, city map, and charter duties.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks about DCP staffing and new positions

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: DCP added 41 new staff in the FY27 executive budget.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: which I've advocated for strongly as a chair, and I really appreciate the administration doing that.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: But it seems like those staff lines were either for managing the city map or for the speed task force.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Did DCP add any new staff to work on neighborhood planning?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So we added about 46 new lines for all of our new responsibilities that are outlined in block by block.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So that includes a number of folks who will be working on our secret exempt applications, which will pull some burden off of our borough offices so that they can better focus their time on neighborhood plans and some of our larger scale planning projects.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: In addition to team to support our work around census, city map, address map, and a number of new charter mandated duties.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: He asks for breakdown of borough staffing and vacancy rates; Garodnick says overall vacancy rate is 24%, with 28 positions posted, 9 in pipeline, and civil service call-ins.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks about DCP vacancy rates and hiring

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Do you have a breakdown of boroughs, staffing, and vacancy rates currently?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So we have an overall vacancy rate of 24%, which is largely driven by the fact that we have 46 new vacancies that we're working to fill.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Right now we have 28 positions posted.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We recently filled, we have nine people in the pipeline for some of our other vacancies, so hiring is a priority.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We also are completing, a lot of our positions at the borough offices are city planning positions that are subject to civil service appointment.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We completed a city civil service call-in this summer.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We have another one coming up in the fall so that we can start to identify candidates from the civil service list and fill those roles as well.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: He asks if DCP can still shape good urban design with pre-certification reduced to six months; Garodnick says speed is about process, not supplementing planning judgment, and projects still go through land use review.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks if DCP can maintain design quality on accelerated track

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The administration released a report on speed task force in May.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The first recommendation of the report was to reduce the time many zoning applications spend in pre-certification from two years to six months.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Highly qualified, well-designed development is essential to success in community support.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Is DCP still able to engage in its work to shape good urban design and quality development on such an accelerated track?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So our work to speed up housing is about improving process.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: It's not about supplementing good planning judgment, quality, or thoughtful review.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We have been working to stand up a new team that will be focused on those seeker-exempt applications.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And again, these are largely applications based on 10 years of analysis that show us less than 1% have an environmental impact, but they've really been sort of held in two years of review.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We're working to accelerate them to six months of pre-certification process, but they will still go through land use review.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: That's where there's an opportunity for us to make sure that we're using sound planning and judgment to evaluate those projects.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so the thoughtful planning work that is essential to the work that we do at DCP, that will continue even as we're working to improve process.

chapters.summary: He asks about the Sprint team; Garodnick says it will focus on SEQRA-exempt applications, work with borough offices, and has 13 exempt applications already, moving to six-month pre-certification in fall.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks about DCP Sprint team goals

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And a part of the fast-tracking work at DCP was the creation of the Sprint team.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Can you describe the planning goals of that team?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And, yeah, can you describe the goals of that team, please?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So I'm excited about our sprint team.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We've been.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: hiring for that team.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And I would just note that there's been a lot of internal and external interest in the roles that we've created for Sprint.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: This is the team that will specifically focus on the pipeline of applications that are exempt from the two-year plus secret review process.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: That team will work in close coordination with other areas of our agency, including with our borough office, so we make sure that they're tapping into that local knowledge and expertise.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We're pulling in folks who have planning experience, planning expertise.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Again, we want to make sure that we're proving process, but we're keeping sound planning judgment front and center in the work that we're doing.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so that team is standing up.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We've already started to identify applications that are exempt in our pipeline today.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So we have about 13 applications that are already exempt.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And in the fall, with our sprint team fully staffed, we will start to move folks towards the six-month pre-certification process.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: He is concerned centralizing work will reduce local consideration; Garodnick says Sprint team works in coordination with borough offices, and borough offices still handle large-scale applications and neighborhood plans.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks about borough office role in private application review

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Will the planners and the urban designers at the DCP borough offices have any role in reviewing private applications going forward?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I'm concerned that centralizing this part of DCP's work will reduce consideration for local neighborhood conditions and priorities.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So I just would note that in creating our sprint team, we went through a pretty extensive process review and reform process.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We didn't hire outside consultants.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We worked internally, bringing in folks from all disciplines and all boroughs across the team to really design.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: this process.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We have a segment of applications that will potentially be exempt from secret review.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: These applications will be led by our sprint team who again will work in coordination and have direct lines of communication.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So what role will the borough office play then?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Sure, so they will have direct lines of communication to our borough offices around applications.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I will note that there's also folks from our borough offices who express interest in joining this team.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So there's a normal exchange between the work that we do in central office and our borough offices.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Our borough offices also have the vast majority of applications that are large scale that have seek review as well as our neighborhood plans, our work with community boards and all the work that we need to do to push our planning agenda forward.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: He notes the goal is ambitious, last achieved in 1920s, asks if they considered additional resources; Garodnick says they have increased headcount and will assess needs in next budget cycle.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks if HPD and DCP have resources for 700,000-unit goal

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: With the administration's recently released the final fair housing growth strategy, a plan completed pursuant to the council's 2023 framework, the goal of 700,000 new housing, that's a very, very ambitious goal.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The last time the city achieved something like that was in the 1920s.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Has HPD and DCP considered the additional resources in staffing, overall budget necessary to achieve the goals of nearly tripling our housing rate?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Just know that the last few years, I think we approved roughly about 80,000 units of housing.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So to get to 700,000 is extremely ambitious.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So have you guys took all that into consideration?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We have our work cut out for us, for sure.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I know as part of the Fair Housing Growth Strategy, our first step is really being able to realize the commitment of 200,000 affordable units as outlined in block by block.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: As noted, we've had an increase in headcount in this last fiscal year in order to achieve that goal, and we will continue to assess our need as we move into the next budget cycle.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: He asks if DCP has done analysis of zoning changes and new development necessary; Garodnick says strategies include citywide TOD, speed reforms, Sprint team, and Affordable Housing Fast Track.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks if DCP analyzed zoning changes needed for housing targets

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Has DCP done an analysis of zoning changes and skills of new development necessary to actually meet these targets?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So some of the zoning, some of the strategies that we're pursuing, right, are really focused on operating at speed and scale.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So citywide TOD approach, which can potentially create a lot of opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: for housing and affordable housing, but also the speed reforms that we just talked about and standing up a sprint team, which would also help us move projects along

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: more quickly, as well as utilizing tools like the Affordable Housing Fast Track, which help us build in places where we haven't seen housing production, affordable housing production in a long time.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so some of these tools, whether they're also making sure we're maximizing the opportunities through City of Yes as well, all of these tools are at play to make sure that we can reach that goal, at least through the work of DCP.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: There's also all of the incredible work that HPD is doing and all the other housing agencies in order to reach that goal.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: He mentions three library sites (Parkchester, Marcy, Sunnyside) and asks if HPD will add them to pipeline; Sandler says they are evaluating, have three library projects already, and will continue conversations.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks HPD to prioritize council-identified library sites

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I want to talk about an initiative that the council has presented, which is libraries.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So the council has identified three additional library sites, one of each in New York, Brooklyn, and Queens Public Libraries, Parchester, Marcy, and Sunnyside.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Where the conditions are right, the sites are largely enough to accommodate HPD's development and a new library.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The existing library needs updates, and the surrounding neighborhood has the right conditions to support density.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Is HPD ready to add these sites to the pipeline and make them a priority?

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you, Council Member, and thank you to the Council for the leadership on identifying these sites and expressing that community support up front.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: That's really important to being able to move these projects forward.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We share the goal of advancing projects that co-locate libraries with affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We have three projects right now that we're advancing through our kind of libraries initiative.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We have the Grand Comp.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: Course Library in the Bronx, the new Utrecht Library in Brooklyn, and the Bloomingdale Library on the Upper West Side.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And these projects are important, and they're also, you know, as part of the housing plan, we're looking at other public facilities that are aging in similar ways and need similar investment.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We've got three for you.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: Yeah, so...

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We're evaluating these sites, we're speaking with the public library systems, and we're eager to continue talking through these opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We have to balance in our pipeline.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So we've been talking about these opportunities, I believe, started early as soon as Speaker Menden came in, when she said she wanted to potentially look at library sites.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We just haven't heard anything back from the administration.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So I understand that you're reviewing the library sites that you're looking at now.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: But there are council members who want to not only upgrade the libraries within their communities, but also add some density.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So I would just ask that on the record, if you guys could actually look at the sites that we're putting to you now to see if we could come up with some form of conversation.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We are looking at the sites.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We've spoken with Council Land just about these specific sites.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We've spoken with the library systems about these specific sites.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We have a long pipeline of sites that we've already committed to communities to develop.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: Like this year, we're working on sites that we've committed to council members to move forward, and we're excited to move those forward and want to figure out how we can fit these into our pipeline.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We need to talk about that some more, but all right.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: He emphasizes homeownership, asks what the plan is; Sandler describes programs: retaining homeowners, down payment assistance (doubling to 300/year, up to 120% AMI), Open Door program (doubling to 300 units/year), and new Our Home program.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks about administration's homeownership plan

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I'm going to go into a question on homeownership.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Then I'm going to go into second round.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Chair, you know how I feel about homeownership.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Ownership is extremely important.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We want to keep New Yorkers in New York City, but I think we focus a lot on rental units, which is extremely important to address the affordability crisis.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: But there are families out there who want to purchase property and actually keep property here to pass down to their families.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: What is the administration's plan on addressing home ownership?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And that could be an HPD and DCP question.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: Sure, I can start.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: You know, HPD is expanding and adding new funding to all of our homeownership programs as part of the Block by Block plan.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We have a multi-pronged strategy for addressing homeownership.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: First is to retain and stabilize existing homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: So that looks like our investments through the Office of the Homeowner Advocate, the Homeowner Help Desk Preservation Programs to support HDFC

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: and Mitchell Llama Co-ops, support for homeowners like HomeFix, which provides loans to keep people in their home and keep existing homeowners there in their homes today that might face displacement pressure.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We're also looking at increasing access to homeownership, primarily through our down payment assistance program, and we're doubling our commitment to that program as well to try to reach...

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: What's the number you're trying to reach?

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: I think it's 300 homeowners a year, up from around 100.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And we've also increased the eligibility from 80% of the area median income to 100%.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: 120% AMI to also have broader reach through that program.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And then on the last side is creating new opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We do that primarily through our open door program, which funds the construction of

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: New construction, affordable co-ops.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We're doubling our production goals on that program from 150 to 300 units a year.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And we're also going to be rolling out a new program soon called Our Home.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We spoke about it in the housing plan.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: This would fund the creation or the preservation of existing buildings that are rental now and converting them into co-ops.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Just to think about it, in the Bronx, it's less than 10% of homeownership.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Is there a target area that you guys are looking for when you're going to be implementing a lot of these programs?

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We do want to focus our homeownership investments in the areas with the lowest rates of homeownership.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So the Bronx is on that list.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I'll stop right there.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I'll go into second rounds of questions.

chapters.summary: He asks what mechanism ensures community board and borough president recommendations meaningfully influence CPC; Garodnick says CPC is independent, reviews all testimony, and commission reports outline how decisions are made.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks how community board recommendations influence CPC decisions

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Councilmember Lewis had to leave, so I'm going to ask this question on behalf of her.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And then next, we're going to go into Councilmember Wong, who's here, and then Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So given that the City Planning Commission rarely, if ever, recommends rejecting or modifying

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: a proposal based on concerns raised by community boards and the borough president, there is a significant concern that the perspective of the communities most directly affected by the land use decision may be disregarded.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: What specific mechanism does the Department of City Planning have in place to ensure that community boards and the borough president's recommendations meaningfully influence the commission's decision?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And will the department commit to great transparency by clearly documenting how?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: These recommendations are considered, addressed, and incorporated into final determinations, particularly when the Commission ultimately disagrees with the recommendation of these local bodies.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So, as you know, the City Planning Commission is an independent commission.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Obviously, we are focused on making sure that we're meeting the needs of New Yorkers and obviously addressing the city's affordable housing crisis.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: By the time an application reaches the City Planning Commission, it has gone through pretty extensive review at the borough president and community board level, as well as the department level for pre-certification.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier in this hearing, there's certainly lots of modifications we see on applications before they reach the CPC, but there still is the ability of the CPC to recommend and make modifications before approval.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Most of the vast majority of affordable housing that we're creating in the city, at least through zoning actions, is done in partnership with the city council.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so we're certainly seeing that the projects that we are approving at the city CPC level are also being approved at the council level.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And to the extent that the council seeks modifications, right, they're coming back to the CPC for final scope determination.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so I think that that exchange will continue as we start to see projects across the city, including in the fast-track districts.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We take every piece of testimony seriously.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We want to make sure that we're listening to community boards and borough presidents.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And our CPC commission reports typically will outline how we arrived at our decision based.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And all the varying factors.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Council Member Wong, followed by Brewer.

chapters.summary: He describes aging power lines and sewer grid, flooding, and asks how DCP will ensure water and electric grids can handle new development; Garodnick says they consider environmental impact and capital infrastructure, and the fast track still includes public review.
chapters.title: Council Member Wong asks about infrastructure and flooding in his district

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Good afternoon, yes.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I live in my district for 50 years.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I moved there in 1976, and I learned two things.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: One, the power cable in front of my house hasn't been changed.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: It's the same cable every morning I looked outside.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So that's one.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And those lines that's been suspended, they're not buried.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And to this day, most of my district, which covers two community boards at your fast track plan, covers this community board four and five.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So the issue is that.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: We're dealing with the same power lines, and worse, we're dealing with the same sewer grid that's been put there for close to 100 years.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So with that, and that there are flood zones in my district, and that the Juniper Valley Park area is low land, is low ground.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: What we used to see is that there's flooding every once every three or four years.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Now is that we see flooding every single time it rains.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And that's serious because, one, the rainwater is nowhere to go, and two, it causes sewer backflows.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And sewer backflows is serious because I see raw sewage literally floating.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: on the streets and it and when the water recedes you smell it for the next couple of days those are serious issues

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: 12 years ago i got scott stringer he was comptroller back back then to come look at this and he says oh yes we got to build more uh basins we gotta we gotta upgrade the sewer lines uh and then

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: We got community boards involved.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Con Ed came, oh yes, the power lines needs to be upgraded.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Nobody mentioned the two words fast tracking.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Oh, we're going to fast track the sewer line upgrades.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Oh, we're going to fast track the power lines.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: All of a sudden, boom, we have fast track building.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Built, built, and built.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Where are you going to find the electricity and where are you going to find the sewer lines that really should be there?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So I even spoke to the mayor, you know, upgrade the infrastructure, then come to tell me about building.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Because we are dealing with these two issues.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Right now with one, two family homes, and they've been there 50, 60, 70 years, okay, that we can't even handle those power requirements or those sewer problems.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Every time there's a windy day, my district lose power because of those power lines that's flapping, flapping in the breeze.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Boom, we lose power.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: It's the truth.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: It's the truth, okay?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And those are, all right, so here's my question, okay?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So I hear all the time from my constituents, even when I

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: work for Robert Holden, right, constituents call that water and electric infrastructures in the area is straining to support the housing that exists today.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: How will DCP ensure that our local water and electric grids can handle the influx of 10-story buildings?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Shouldn't we be improving infrastructure before allowing new development?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Please answer that.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you for your question, and thank you for bringing those issues to you.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I'm sorry that your district is experiencing that and certainly want to make sure that we have a better handle on what's happening there.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: As I noted throughout this hearing, we want to make sure that as we're considering housing opportunities and communities, we're also looking at the environmental impact needed capital infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I would just also note that we're planning for a growth of housing, but we are way behind in terms of the housing we need for the growth in population that we've already seen.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: The city has grown.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: People are here.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: They're living in homeless shelters.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: They are underhoused.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: They are doubled up in apartments.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: What we also need to do is ensure that we're building the housing that people need today while we're also planning for the housing that people need in the future, including folks who may be in your district but not in the housing that they need.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so through the fast track, we have an opportunity to be able to accelerate the production of affordable housing in your district while also still ensuring public review, community board review, an assessment of your physical and capital infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And we certainly will be attentive to those needs as we start to plan forward.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And I would just note that we are also looking at opportunities, again, relative to your communities.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We don't have an expectation that the South Shore of Staten Island looks like Midtown Manhattan, right?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We want to make sure that growth makes sense in that community and that the community is able to accommodate it.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah, growth makes sense when the infrastructure could accommodate it.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Without talking the infrastructure and you just keep telling people to come in and build, you're putting the carriage in front of the horse.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And that's the message I want to relay today.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: Councilmember Brewer.

chapters.summary: She asks if the administration commits to not tearing down rent-stabilized buildings, says buyouts happen, and asks about historic districts; Garodnick says they want to protect rent-stabilized housing and historic districts go through LPC review.
chapters.title: Council Member Brewer asks about rent-stabilized demolition and historic districts

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Are you committing to saying you're not going to tear down rent-stabilized buildings?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Let me tell you what happens.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Excel, just empty 96th Street and Broadway.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So they didn't have any discussion.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They just paid money.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: 84th Street and Columbus, they just paid money.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick

utterances.text: So there are laws that do prohibit...

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I will say that there are...

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: There are those protections, but there's also the work that we're doing to make sure that we protect tenants as an administration.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I would just note that includes expanding investment in right to counsel, baselining it for $40 million.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: I can't listen to it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer

utterances.text: So whether it's the fast track or any other land use action, any proposals that impact historic districts will still go through the existing LPC review process.

utterances.text: You know how I feel about that process right now with West Park Presbyterian Church being torn down, proposed.

chapters.summary: She asks why the Bloomingdale Library project is only partially affordable while the other two are 100%; Garodnick says the other two are 100% affordable, and the Bloomingdale site can cross-subsidize; Sandler says they lack capital resources and use creative strategies.
chapters.title: Council Member Brewer asks why Bloomingdale Library is only partially affordable

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Bloomingdale Library.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Yes, Michael, but why is it only partially going to be affordable?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Are the other two libraries 100%?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Are we the only one that is partially?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: The other two libraries are 100% affordable.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Oh, how did I guess?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: On sites that can accommodate really significant density and that have the opportunity for the non-affordable units to cross-subsidize the creation of the new capital needs of that facility.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Then why do you say we want to build in areas like Board 7 but not really to the max?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because that's what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You're saying we're on city-owned land, but we're not going to take advantage.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We're going to the Bronx like you always do.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We don't want to build.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Affordable, really, in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's what you're saying, when you're only doing MIH to 25%.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We're not only doing MIH to 25% in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We do have 100% affordable projects.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: At this library.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We have WISFISH project in your community, and we do want to finance 100% affordable housing in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: But it's not.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's only 25%.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: So the city has a lot of aging facilities across the city.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: We do not have the capital resources to maintain all of the city's resources and amenities.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And we need to use creative strategies that can finance the replacement of these facilities.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: Efficiently and with limited strain on the city's resources.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I just want to be clear that I want 100% at that library, and the city is saying no, just so we're on the record.

chapters.summary: She says Harborview has been waiting since Hudson Yards decision for 124 units, asks for commitment; Sandler says they are focused on preserving existing NYCHA units, and Harborview has not moved forward; Brewer asks about Hudson Yards agreement.
chapters.title: Council Member Brewer asks about NYCHA Harborview units

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Also, NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have lots of NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We don't want to be building.

utterances.text: Harborview has been waiting since the Hudson Yards decision, 124 units.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Everybody at HPD knows about it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Nobody's done a damn thing about it.

utterances.text: NICHA, Harborview, since Hudson Yards when I signed off for that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And I want a commitment that we're not going to tear down trees and get rid of all the open space that NICHA buildings have.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: Yeah, well, certainly I can't speak for NICHA.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: I will say that our collaborations with NICHA, and I think the city's focus on NICHA, has been protecting the existing units that exist.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And so we've been focused on our NICHA preservation projects, on infill that supports the preservation of existing NICHA.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer

utterances.text: We'll have to speak with Nisha about that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They blame it on HPD.
