utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Brewer.

chapters.summary: He reads a statement about 1880 East Tremont Avenue, originally planned for housing but now slated for a school, and asks what process assesses co-locating housing with schools; Sandler describes the Mayor's LIFT initiative and interagency coordination.
chapters.title: Chair Riley reads Council Member Farias' question on school site co-location

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I have a statement by Councilmember Farias that I'm going to read and then ask you guys a question.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The block-by-block report states that one of its goals is to maximize the potential of city-owned land, including school properties as sites that can support new housing.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: My question concerns 1880 East Tremont Avenue in the Bronx, located near White Plains Road.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: As a part of the Bronx Metro North Rezoning, this site was expected to be developed with over 500 units of new housing with at least 125 affordable units,

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: along with publicly accessible open space and neighborhood serving retail.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: However, the majority of the site is now slated for a development as a school.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: When the city plans new schools on city-owned property, what process is used to assess opportunities for co-locating housing?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Is there a formal framework or set of criteria used to evaluate whether a site can accommodate both educational and residential uses?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And how will the city ensure that publicly owned sites are being evaluated?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: comprehensively so that opportunities to produce housing are not missed when other public facilities are planned.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And once again, this is Councilmember Amanda Farias from the Council District 18 asking this question.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: I can speak a little bit to the Mayor's LIFT initiative, the Land Inventory Fast Track.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: This was an executive order issued on day one of the administration.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: The executive order tasks us with looking comprehensively at the city's assets to evaluate which assets can be

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: used to develop affordable housing or housing generally.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And as part of that executive order, it also ordered that agencies pursuing capital projects on city-owned assets have to coordinate with the list task force to evaluate the opportunity for housing.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: So that coordination is happening now as a result of this task force.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And we have DCAS and a number of different agencies, including HPD, EDC, Department of City Planning, who are all looking at city-owned sites.

utterances.speaker: Michael Sandler
utterances.text: And then as different capital projects are coming through on or proposed capital projects on city-owned sites, we're looking at should this project move forward or should we be looking at housing and co-location in addition to that facility?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Well, originally this site was supposed to be housing, and now they're talking about...

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Majority of yeah I'm not familiar with the exact site so I'll have to follow up and look into that okay all right

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: okay if you guys could look into it because this we held the process community input many community members thought that this was going to be housing opportunities and now it's going to be

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: a school which we embrace and welcome new schools of course um talking to any other council members you could tell them that they are trying to get as much new schools in the district as possible

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: but specifically for council member faris this was something that was supposed to happen in a district so if you could just follow up with her because um it's a concern to that community yeah we'll follow up with council member faris

chapters.summary: He asks if DCP is continuing to implement the industrial plan; Garodnick says yes, they use the land use framework to guide planning, and balance housing in neighborhood industrial areas while preserving heavy industrial.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks about implementation of New York City Industrial Plan

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: In December 2025, DCP released a New York City industrial plan as required by Local Law 172 of 2023.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The plan includes the first time a citywide land use framework for industrial areas, as well as numerous important recommendations for economic development policy and infrastructure investment.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Is DCP continuing to work on implementing the recommendation of the New York City Industrial Plan?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So we've been utilizing the land use framework and the industrial plan to help guide our planning activities as well as decisions that we make, including at the CPC.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so there's a framework in the industrial plan that outlines primary, secondary, and neighborhood industrial areas,

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: primary being our most intensive manufacturing uses, neighborhood industrial areas serving as the areas where we already see sort of mixed-use activity between residential, commercial, light manufacturing, for instance.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so we've seen and certainly have pursued housing opportunities in some of the neighborhood industrial areas while we have certainly been working to ensure that we are keeping our heavy industrial.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: areas intact.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: That framework has been really important and helpful to how we are considering the work that we do.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We know there are a number of other recommendations in the industrial plan, particularly recommendations that are more programmatic policy.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so we certainly have been in conversations with our other city agency partners in the economic development and justice world who are also looking at those proposals.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And how will the initiatives and blah, blah, blah be balanced with the goals of the New York City industrial plan and the preservation of dedicated manufacturing zone land?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Yeah, I think the industrial plan for the first time in a while gives us a framework to utilize as we start to reach this goal towards 200,000 new units, right, by sort of designating what we see as primary and secondary industrial where we,

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: and versus what we see as neighborhood industrial, which are areas that are more appropriate for including housing, closer to transit, have much more walkability.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We're able to factor those neighborhoods in more appropriately to our housing planning opportunities while still making sure that we are securing the jobs, right, and the protections that we need in our industrial sector.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: He asks if DCP and HPD are looking at activating more waterfronts; Garodnick says there is tension with industrial uses, but they evaluate proposals, ensure public access, and recently surveyed New Yorkers on waterfront activation.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks about activating more waterfronts for housing

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And within the Fair Housing Growth Strategy Plan, I know we talked about homeownership and other kinds of housing.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Activating waterfronts.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Is DCP, HPD looking at possibly activating more waterfronts?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I only ask this because I know I get a ton of requests from people who are coming into my office who don't want to go to New Jersey because New Jersey.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: has put a lot of development on waterfront, and typically a lot more people would like those amenities to live by a waterfront and have that open space.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So is there any mindset on creating more residential areas around waterfront?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I know the majority of WIP is focused on North Shore, but is there any other plans to activate any waterfronts?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, I think there's some level of tension, right?

chapters.summary: He asks how DCP and HPD will collaborate on senior housing, affordable rental, and homeownership in White Plains Road; Garodnick says they will work closely with HPD, have heard community needs, and will figure out mix of programs.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks about White Plains Road plan collaboration

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: A lot of our industrials traditionally along the waterfront, in addition to housing opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so we see a mix of waterfront communities where there's heavy industrial as well as communities that significant housing has been built along the waterfront, including

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: in the Bronx waterfront where we see a lot more projects emerging along the Harlem River.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: At DCP, it's been important for us to ensure that we're evaluating those proposals appropriately relative to the need, that we're making sure that public access along the waterfront remains with private development,

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: and that we have also recently conducted a survey of New Yorkers to also get their input on the waterfront so we can think about ways to activate that beyond housing.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: All right, my last set of questions, White Plains Road.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I wasn't going to leave without that, right?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: All right, so Councilmember Dinois and myself have been engaging with DCP regarding White Plains Road.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: How will City Plan and HPD collaborate to develop a plan that promotes senior housing, affordable rental housing, and affordable homeownership opportunities?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We have the Ebenezer location, HPD, that's for you, that we've been seeing a lot of challenges with.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: But how will City Plan and HPD collaborate to develop a plan that promotes senior housing, affordable rental housing, and affordable homeownership opportunities tailored to the area's needs,

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: particularly given that our local median household income is below the citywide median household income?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And I know I mentioned this earlier in our hearing, but really appreciate your partnership on White Plains Road and all the attention and detail that you've given as we started that planning process.

chapters.summary: He says they have had challenges with HPD regarding Ebenezer, asks them to sit down with the organization; HPD (unknown speaker) says they would be happy to meet and have technical assistance programs.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks HPD to meet with Ebenezer church on affordable homeownership

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We will work very closely with HPD on our approach to White Plains Road.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We know the AMI in that community.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We also have started to hear.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: from community members, the types of housing needs that they have.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: Right now, we have been focused on figuring out what the potential is along the corridor, as you know, just in terms of growth, right?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And then we can start to figure out what are the mix of housing programs that can be activated when we have a zoning that aligns with the corridor's needs.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so as part of any neighborhood plan,

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: all of our agency partners at the table, HPD in particular, and they certainly will be at the table in the work that we do in White Plains Road.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Well, typically with the Ebenezer plan, because we have a plan on White Plains Road that wants to put home ownership, we are having a challenge speaking to HPD regarding the issues that Ebenezer is seeing.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So I would just, on the record, ask you guys for probably the 20th time, if you guys could come to the table and sit down with the organization to address that cause with the Ebenezer church location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sorry if I'm personally not familiar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I mean, this is a faith-based organization that wants to develop on their land?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Oh, we would be happy to meet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I would say on the record, yes, we would love to meet with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We've done a lot of work to support faith-based organizations in developing affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We recently launched a new...

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Well, this one is affordable home ownership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're happy to speak with them about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we recently launched a technical assistance program with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're going to be funding a new technical assistance program with Enterprise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we launched a series of classes for faith-based organizations and are happy to meet with them.

chapters.summary: He asks how HPD will encourage family-sized units; HPD says design standards require minimum 30% two-to-three bedrooms, max 25% studios, and they typically exceed, closer to 41% two or more bedrooms.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks how HPD will prioritize family-sized units in rezoning

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Councilmember Dinos and I have consistently emphasized the need for greater ratio of family-sized housing units.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: If proposed rezoning is approved, how would HPD work with developers to encourage and prioritize the inclusion of units that could accommodate families and support the long-term needs of the community?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: HPDS design standards for new construction projects that are based on population data.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We require a minimum of 30% two to three bedrooms, a maximum of 25% studios.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We typically exceed these looking at data about our projects.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We're closer to 41% financing two or more bedrooms as part of the rezoning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And as part of our conversations about future projects, we're happy to keep discussing what's the right bedroom mix for an individual project.

chapters.summary: He asks how the city will incorporate community input on size and scale; Garodnick says they are pulling together a draft zoning framework, will continue engagement, and will move into public review.
chapters.title: Chair Riley asks how community vision will shape White Plains Road zoning

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: As we approach the conclusion of the community engagement phase, how is the city planning to incorporate the community's shared vision into the zoning framework that facilitates much-needed affordable housing while balancing the community's input on size and scale of buildings?

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So, although we've been engaging community for quite some time, that will continue significantly.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So, right now we are at the stage, as you know, Councilmember, of starting to really pull together a draft zoning framework.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We have not moved into public review yet with that project and taking your feedback, Councilmember Dinowitz, as well as the working group and community before we can even really move forward with a study.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: And so we are incorporating what we heard from community members around the need for growth.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: As you know, I joined you and members of the community on our walk shop, and we walked through the neighborhood to really figure out.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: the different nodes and connections within White Plains Road where we can accommodate much more growth, but also places where we know there's sensitivity based on homeowners and other sorts of low-scale characteristics of the neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So that work is underway.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We have been in conversation, right, to make sure that we're figuring out a draft zoning that really makes sense, but we really need to have conversation with community members first to really get to where we need.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: We will then move that into public review and start studying the zoning while we also talk about all of the other components of the project, jobs, commercial vitalization, street safety, public realm, all of the things that are critical to a neighborhood plan.

utterances.speaker: Dan Garodnick
utterances.text: So we have a long road ahead of continued conversations with you as well as with the community.

chapters.summary: He thanks witnesses, says the essence is collaboration and planning, the council is not NIMBY, wants to work with administration, but needs comprehensive planning and infrastructure investment; 700,000 units is ambitious and they need partnership.
chapters.title: Chair Riley delivers closing remarks on collaboration and comprehensive planning

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: And thank you for answering our questions here today.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I think the essence of today's conversation was focused on collaboration and planning.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We understand the crisis.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We are not the council that is the NIMBYs.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We want to actually work with the administration, but there has to be some sense of urban or comprehensive planning that's coming into effect.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: It's unfair to just focus on units and building and just putting people in a location where there's no true investment on infrastructure, on the schools, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I think everyone in this room would like to live in a vibrant community.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We talk a lot about affordable New York City, but we need a livable New York City.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We could be extremely affordable, but we don't put people in a community that they can actually live in and thrive in.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: That's where.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We're going to lose a lot more New Yorkers to other states, and we don't want to do that.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We are in a very important time.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We understand the work that we have to do in the council.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: 700,000 units is extremely ambitious.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We want to work with you guys.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So that's just what we want to emphasize with this conversation today.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We do want to hear something more with the plans that you guys put out.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: How do you guys plan to achieve these goals?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Because these are very ambitious goals and you're going to need a partner to achieve these goals.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So please utilize us as a partner.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: We have council members that are trying to do their fair share, but they need the collaboration and cooperation with the administration.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Council Member, are you good?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: All right, wrong question.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Do you have any more questions?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Okay, good.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: He supports Block by Block's goals but says comprehensive planning is missing; calls for legislation for community-based neighborhood planning and coordination with neighborhood investment.
chapters.title: Chris Walters of ANHD testifies on comprehensive planning

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Walters
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Walters
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair and committee members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Walters
utterances.text: My name is Chris Walters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Walters
utterances.text: I'm the Associate Director for Policy and Research at the Association for Neighborhood and Housing Development, A&HD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Walters
utterances.text: I'll just give a top-line summary of our more detailed written testimony, which we'll submit to you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Walters
utterances.text: We believe Block by Block is an ambitious plan that needs to be supported by comprehensive planning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Walters
utterances.text: We support its goals of both creating and preserving 200,000 affordable homes and its recognition of the need for a more equitable distribution of affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Walters
utterances.text: However, building more affordable housing, while essential, is not enough on its own.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Walters
utterances.text: As you all have raised today, New Yorkers need affordable homes and neighborhoods with the infrastructure, services, jobs, and amenities that allow communities to thrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Walters
utterances.text: And they deserve a meaningful role in deciding how their neighborhoods grow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Walters
utterances.text: We believe that comprehensive planning is the missing tool that can connect these goals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Walters
utterances.text: I failed to mention as well, we also convened the Thriving Communities Coalition, which is a citywide coalition working to advance land use justice and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Walters
utterances.text: We urge the Mamdani administration to fulfill his campaign commitment to comprehensive planning and build on the strengths of block by block by addressing three critical gaps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Walters
utterances.text: First, planning must begin with an accurate assessment of housing needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Walters
utterances.text: We believe the administration's recently released Fair Housing Growth Strategy falls short of providing that assessment, particularly for the needs of low-income households.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Walters
utterances.text: Second, housing growth must be coordinated with neighborhood investment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Walters
utterances.text: And third, communities must be empowered as equal partners in planning with meaningful opportunities to put forward their proactive plans to shape local development that meets citywide needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Walters
utterances.text: To help advance these goals, we would make the following call to City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Walters
utterances.text: We would love to work with you alongside the Thriving Communities Coalition to advance legislation establishing a meaningful community-based neighborhood planning process and establish a clear pathway for their consideration and implementation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Walters
utterances.text: And second, we would like to work with you all to help develop neighborhood plans in your district, as many of you are doing already.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Walters
utterances.text: In conclusion, again, we believe comprehensive planning can help reconcile the urgency of housing production with the equally important goals of community participation, equitable investment, and neighborhood stability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Chris Walters
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your consideration.

chapters.summary: She echoes need for comprehensive planning, says deeply affordable housing numbers won't meet Brooklyn's needs, and concerns about displacement risk and preservation of M zones.
chapters.title: Lacey Tauber of Brooklyn Borough President's Office testifies on fair housing and affordability

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Lacey Tauber.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: I'm the Director of Legislative Affairs and Climate Initiatives for Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: And I just want to echo what Chris just said.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: It was really exciting to hear you talk about the need for

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: comprehensive planning because that's something that the BP has been advocating for for a really long time and we would also love to work with you on potentially developing some legislation to meet that need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: And so I will summarize our comments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: So block by block states that the housing shortage is worse for those who earn the least, which is true.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: However, according to what they're calling for, there would only be 25,500 new homes over the next five years available citywide, you know, assuming full implementation for those with very low and extremely low incomes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: The median household income in Brooklyn is about $84,000, which is $7,600 less than the 60% AMI threshold for a family of three.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: So we acknowledge that there are structural barriers to producing deeply affordable housing, but these numbers simply won't meet the needs in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: On the fair housing growth strategy, we were happy to see that HPD significantly improved its methodology, but there are still some factors required in the law that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: they haven't considered in getting to the numbers they put out, including displacement risk, access to employment opportunities, open space, and other neighborhood amenities and public services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: And we're just concerned that the targets continue to call upon the highest growth neighborhoods to add the most housing, while the lowest growth neighborhoods will continue to do the least.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: So it calls for also local planning processes to meet these needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: Again, we're concerned about the absence of a coordinated citywide comprehensive plan that includes spatial guidance and an implementation framework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: And without that, you know, really the targets are just ideas and politics can drive decision making.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: We want to really quickly just also want to mention that we want to make sure that a housing development doesn't come at the expense of the worker.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: And we want to see our M zones preserved, creating access to job opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lacey Tauber
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: He says recent changes are steps in right direction but more needed; supports neighborhood rezonings, micro plans, and transit-oriented development.
chapters.title: Brendan Cheney of New York Housing Conference testifies on housing supply

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: My name is Brendan Cheney.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: I'm Director of Policy and Operations at the New York Housing Conference.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: I've submitted our full testimony in writing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: I will summarize in the interest of time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: As we've heard today, throughout the hearing, New York City is facing an ongoing housing crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: Recent changes to increase housing supply are steps in the right direction, but we need to do more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: The city of yes, zoning changes, last year's ballot changes will all generate additional housing in neighborhoods across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: But these two efforts alone will not allow us to add all the housing we need to address the crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: In the fair housing growth strategy, the mayor projected the city needs an additional 700,000 units over the next 10 years, including 200,000 units of new affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: There are massive unmet housing needs in every neighborhood across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: There's not enough opportunities for homeownership or rental housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: Young adults starting out, families with children, older adults, all don't have enough housing choice, facing limited options and high costs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: No community board is immune from this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: Housing affordability is a problem at every income level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: We will not see the housing growth we need in all neighborhoods without further changes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: And this is why we support the zoning changes and planning proposals in block by block.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: Further neighborhood rezonings, including micro plans, are necessary to expand development across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: Neighborhood rezonings are a powerful way to add housing supply in a way that meets neighborhood needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: Adding transit-oriented...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: to development to more neighborhoods is also necessary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: The program passed as part of the city of yes will be helpful, but it can go further.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: We look forward to working with the administration, the city council to support further changes and to support affordable housing and housing growth throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: I'm happy to answer any questions.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: He supports Block by Block, focuses on ADUs, says over 256,000 lots could accommodate ADUs, recommends expanding ADU Plus program and community-based nonprofits for technical assistance.
chapters.title: Kevin Wolf of Center for NYC Neighborhoods testifies on ADUs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Riley, for having this hearing and the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: My name is Kevin Wolf, and I'm the Director of Policy and Research for the Center for New York City Neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: As one of the largest homeowner service nonprofit organizations, we do support the goals of the block-by-block housing plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: I do want to echo what my colleagues have said today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: We wanted to specifically focus on ADUs as a central part of the strategy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: We've done a research report and our research has identified that there are over 256,000 residential lots in the city that could feasibly accommodate an ADU under the new zoning provisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: These could include basement apartments, attics, garage apartments, backyard and backyard cottages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: Queens has the greatest potential.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: Almost half of those eligible lots are in Queens, but there are significant opportunities in the Bronx, Brooklyn and Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: From our research, ADUs can be less expensive to build the multifamily housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: While also keeping the content.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: architecture of the neighborhood, providing rental income that helps homeowners manage their maintenance costs, preserve homes, and help those age in place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: They can also create rental housing that is affordable within neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: So we believe that the city should look at high potential neighborhoods, but also look at areas that have lower displacement risk, ensuring that longtime homeowners can remain in their homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: One of the key issues that we find is that the homeowners are lacking the financing, the technical expertise, and the support to navigate the new construction around an ADU.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: So we recommend expanding the ADU Plus program and also investing in community-based nonprofits to help guide homeowners through the process, as well as continuing the centralized city resources for technical assistance,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: permitting, and financing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: And we've submitted our written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Wolf
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: There being no questions, thank you so much for your testimony here today.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Next, we'll have Matt Thibodeau, Yvette Shen, Jack Connors, and Howard Slaykin.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Matt Thibodeau?

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Go ahead.

chapters.summary: He supports ambition but concerns about lack of coordination, rigor, and strategy; urges city to publish clear plan connecting housing goals with capital commitments and establish dedicated funding for neighborhood planning.
chapters.title: Matt Thibodeau of Municipal Arts Society testifies on comprehensive planning

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Thibodeau
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Riley and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Thibodeau
utterances.text: My name is Matt Thibodeau.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Thibodeau
utterances.text: I'm an urban planner at the Municipal Arts Society of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Thibodeau
utterances.text: MAS has long advocated for comprehensive community-based planning that pairs housing growth with neighborhood services and climate resilient infrastructure, both independently and as a longstanding member of the Thriving Communities Coalition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Thibodeau
utterances.text: We support Mayor Mamdani's ambition to build more affordable homes, but have significant concerns about the lack of coordination, rigor, and strategy for community-based implementation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Thibodeau
utterances.text: Block by block, the Fair Housing Growth Strategy and the Affordable Housing Fast Track are advancing on separate paths.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Thibodeau
utterances.text: It is unclear how they fit together or how 700,000 new homes will be matched by the schools, parks, transit, or flood protection they require.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Thibodeau
utterances.text: Block by Block lays out an ambitious vision, but offers few details on delivery.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Thibodeau
utterances.text: The report does not explain considerations that will guide future land use actions, such as transit-oriented development or comprehensive neighborhood plans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Thibodeau
utterances.text: We urge the city to publish a clear plan that connects housing goals with capital commitments to public infrastructure and communities that are expected to densify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Thibodeau
utterances.text: Likewise, the Fair Housing Growth Strategy lacks detail on where and how communities will accommodate growth and what types of housing New Yorkers actually need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Thibodeau
utterances.text: The report does not respond to the full intent of Local Law 167, which explicitly requires a detailed housing needs assessment and consideration of transit, public services, and climate impacts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Thibodeau
utterances.text: We urge HPD to deepen its housing needs analysis to quantify the levels of affordability needed by each community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Thibodeau
utterances.text: as well as to outline district-level spatial plans to guide development to areas with the capacity to handle additional density.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Thibodeau
utterances.text: Finally, the 12 districts identified for the affordable housing fast track have no accompanying planning strategy or spatial framework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Thibodeau
utterances.text: The city must thoughtfully determine where new housing will be sited in these 12 districts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Thibodeau
utterances.text: We urge the city to establish dedicated funding for neighborhood planning with a clear pathway to implementation, as it has in the past with the Neighborhood Development Fund.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Thibodeau
utterances.text: MAS welcomes the opportunity to set up a time to discuss additional details.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Matt Thibodeau
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Matt Yvette.

chapters.summary: She focuses on accessibility, enforcement of fair housing laws, funding for CCHR to enforce source of income discrimination, and comprehensive planning.
chapters.title: Yvette Chen of Fair Housing Justice Center testifies on accessibility and discrimination

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvette Chen
utterances.text: Good afternoon, my name is Yvette Chen and I'm a policy associate at the Fair Housing Justice Center, a civil rights nonprofit organization serving the NYC area.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvette Chen
utterances.text: Our mission is to eliminate housing discrimination, promote accessible and inclusive communities, and strengthen the enforcement of fair housing laws.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvette Chen
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvette Chen
utterances.text: We welcome the administration's initiative to address the city's deeply inequitable housing crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvette Chen
utterances.text: However, building new affordable housing will not in itself produce housing equity or be effective without the enforcement of fair housing laws.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvette Chen
utterances.text: I will focus on three priorities today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvette Chen
utterances.text: First, accessibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvette Chen
utterances.text: The city must act urgently because disability discrimination is rampant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvette Chen
utterances.text: DOB and HPD must work together to review plans and inspect new developments, rather than relying on self-certification, which lets violations go undetected.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvette Chen
utterances.text: The city should also enforce the 5% UFAS requirement, bar non-compliant developers from subsidies and approvals, and target retrofits to buildings with documented complaints.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvette Chen
utterances.text: Second, discrimination will persist without the enforcement of the human rights law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvette Chen
utterances.text: We ask the council to urge the administration to fund and support CCHR to eliminate source of income discrimination and enforce the Fair Transfer Housing Act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvette Chen
utterances.text: SOI discrimination has been illegal since 2008, yet it's ceased.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvette Chen
utterances.text: CCHR's most common complaint.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvette Chen
utterances.text: The Fair Transfer Housing Act took effect in January 2025, yet CCHR received no additional funding to enforce the law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvette Chen
utterances.text: Without adequate funding to enforce the law, vouchers will go unused and thwart the city's housing mobility strategy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvette Chen
utterances.text: Lastly, invest in fair housing education and coordinate growth with neighborhood investment and real community participation through comprehensive planning so that new housing is paired with the infrastructure and services neighborhoods need to thrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvette Chen
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: He says crisis is due to not building enough homes, supports 200,000 affordable homes goal, and cross-subsidizing MIH with market rate; looks forward to TOD citywide.
chapters.title: Jack Connors of Open New York testifies on housing shortage

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: I'm Jack Connors, City Legislative Manager at Open New York, a statewide grassroots advocacy group that fights for more homes of all kinds, protections for tenants, and an all-of-the-above approach to solving our housing affordability crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: Thank you to Chair Riley and members of the committee for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: Our housing crisis is rooted in the fact that we simply do not build enough homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: Displacement, exclusion, tenant harassment, and homelessness are all exacerbated by our dire housing shortage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: Homeownership is out of reach for everybody but the wealthiest, and tenants have far too few options, a fact borne out by data that landlords are well aware of.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: New York, our housing vacancy rate is at a historically low 1.4%, just 0.4% for our deepest, most deeply affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: And the predictable result of this is a city where an astounding 86% of New Yorkers making less than 50K are rent burdened, and 68% are severely rent burdened, spending more than half of their pre-tax income on rent alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: This housing scarcity empowers landlords and exacerbates every other affordability challenge we face, disproportionately impacting lower income populations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: We also face a challenging financial atmosphere, with the federal government further retreating from its already limited role in making housing affordable and the cost of borrowing continuing to climb.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: We applaud the goal of building 200,000 new affordable homes in the next decade, as well as the mayor and the council's historic capital funding for HPD, which will allow 8,000

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: and more affordable units to be subsidized.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: Yet this figure also highlights the challenges posed by relying on city funding alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: By cross-subsidizing MIH homes with market rate in the highest demand areas, the city can build more of the affordable housing New Yorkers need while reserving city subsidy for the places where it's needed most.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: This funding mechanism works.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: MIH tenants benefit from homes that remain affordable decades into the future, and market rate homes reduce displacement pressure on our already limited stock of deeply affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: Looking forward, we look forward to the opportunity to engage with the council to help legalize TOD citywide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Connors
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you for testifying.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I think the message from the first panel on this panel, I think no one's objected to the mayor's plan.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: I think we just focus on a more comprehensive plan on how we're going to get there.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: It's easy enough to give a projection of numbers, but actually obtaining those numbers is not truly easy if it's not some form of collaboration.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So I appreciate all of you coming here.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Outside of here, you all have been a collaborative partner as well.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: So thank you so much for taking the time to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: The next panel we're going to hear from consists of Victoria Hoffer, Josephine Beckman, Rochelle Thompson, and Stephanie Simone Mahoney.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: She's next.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: We'll begin first with Stephanie.

chapters.summary: She objects to CB10 being on fast track, says methodology is flawed, concerns about displacement and loss of democratic accountability.
chapters.title: Stephanie Simone-Mahaney of Brooklyn CB10 testifies on fast track methodology

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Simone-Mahaney
utterances.text: I'm Stephanie Simone Mahaney and the chair of the Zoning and Land Use Committee of Brooklyn Community Board 10, representing Bay Ridge, Diker Heights, and Fort Hamilton.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Simone-Mahaney
utterances.text: CB10 has been identified as the lowest producing district among the 12 designated for affordable housing fast track.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Simone-Mahaney
utterances.text: We take serious exception to both the methodology used to reach that designation and the consequences it carries for our community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Simone-Mahaney
utterances.text: A five-year measure of newly produced income-restricted housing divided by a district's existing housing units is not a meaningful measure of its development capacity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Simone-Mahaney
utterances.text: Existing housing stock does not tell us how much land is available or appropriate for development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Simone-Mahaney
utterances.text: The formula does not adequately account for existing density, vacant land, contextual zoning, infrastructure constraints, or the feasibility of producing affordable housing in a largely built-out district like ours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Simone-Mahaney
utterances.text: Nor does it recognize the considerable value of preserving existing affordable and rent-stabilized housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Simone-Mahaney
utterances.text: We're particularly concerned that the pursuit of new affordable housing could come at the expense of the affordable housing we already have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Simone-Mahaney
utterances.text: Upzoning creates development opportunities, but it can also place existing lower cost and rent-stabilized housing under redevelopment pressure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Simone-Mahaney
utterances.text: The potential loss of existing affordability must be considered alongside anticipated gains in new production.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Simone-Mahaney
utterances.text: Low affordable housing production does not necessarily indicate unmet affordable housing need, nor does it establish that additional development would deliver affordability to those who need it most.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Simone-Mahaney
utterances.text: The affordability crisis and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Simone-Mahaney
utterances.text: the housing shortage should not be treated as synonyms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Simone-Mahaney
utterances.text: Increasing supply does not by itself guarantee affordability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Simone-Mahaney
utterances.text: Equally troubling for us is the loss of democratic accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Simone-Mahaney
utterances.text: Under the Affordable Housing Fast Track, final approval rests with the CPC, a body of appointed officials, rather than the city council members elected to represent the affected communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Simone-Mahaney
utterances.text: While commissioners have citywide planning responsibilities, they cannot be expected to possess the same familiarity with our neighborhoods, infrastructure, or longstanding community concerns as those who represent work within them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Simone-Mahaney
utterances.text: Just to say, community boards and borough presidents retain opportunity to comment, but their role is further diminished in a compressed process that removes final approval authority from locally elected representatives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Simone-Mahaney
utterances.text: And I would just like to thank you for the opportunity to speak.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Simone-Mahaney
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Victoria?

chapters.summary: She describes Bay Ridge's history, says MIH rents are above market, and the definition of affordability is biased against stable communities.
chapters.title: Victoria Hoffmel of Bay Ridge testifies on neighborhood planning and affordability

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: Hi, I'm Victoria Hoffmel.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: I'm a resident of Bay Ridge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: I'm just going to talk about my neighborhood because I feel like every neighborhood is specific and unique, and I think that's how we have to look at it, and I don't feel this process is such.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: So about 20 years ago, I worked with Councilman Gentile Teresa on Bay Ridge at the suggestion of the New York City Planning Department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: Volunteers went block by block carefully, creating a balance between the needs of residents, community facilities, and businesses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: That has been revoked from us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: At the same time, a representative's voice is being eliminated from the land use process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: It's very undemocratic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: My neighborhood also provides services to New Yorkers who live way beyond our boundaries through our plethora of schools, medical facilities, places of employment, senior services, and supportive housing for seniors and developmentally delayed adults.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: We are lucky to have a mixed housing stock as a result of the immigrants who built it, believing in a social contract and in decent housing for all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: As a result, our communities economically, ethnically, and age diverse, and remains one of the most affordable and stable neighborhoods in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: At the same time, we have retained many rent-controlled apartments, and there are a few empty lots on which to develop.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: For our largesse, we had approximately 800 homes raised and 7,000 residents displaced with the Verrazano Bridge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: When they got to the neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: We were then amputated from the rest of our community's Sunset Park through redlining.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: We are taxed 60% more for properties that are worth less in downtown Brooklyn, have been charged so for more than four decades, and now find ourselves one of the 12 neighborhoods, senselessly and I would argue illegally, listed

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: on the chopping block of communities that need to provide more affordable housing through new construction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: I'd like to explain some of the current policies, how they're actually raising prices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: The mandatory inclusion in housing, the studio goes for approximately $500 to $1,300 above our market rate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: This in turn will further raise our property values and increase our unfair taxes, impacting both homeowners and renters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: The definition of affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: Affordability is now being defined by how many new housing units have been constructed in the last five years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: This definition is ludicrous, and if you notice, mentions nothing about what housing actually costs and nothing about our actual housing reality, but everything about real estate interests.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: It is also biased against stable and already affordable communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: I have some suggestions of what would help make our neighborhoods and other communities more affordable, but I'll send those in online.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Victoria Hoffmel
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: You can also give that to the sergeant, and I'll take a look at that, Victoria.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Next, Josephine, followed by Rochelle.

chapters.summary: She says CB10 has 14,909 rent-stabilized units, concerns about displacement, school seat deficit, and antiquated sewer infrastructure.
chapters.title: Josephine Beckmann of Brooklyn CB10 testifies on infrastructure and displacement

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josephine Beckmann
utterances.text: Yes, it's on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josephine Beckmann
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Riley.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josephine Beckmann
utterances.text: My name is Joseph.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josephine Beckmann
utterances.text: I am the district manager of Community Board 10 in encompassing the neighborhoods of Bay Ridge, Diker Heights, and Fort Hamilton.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josephine Beckmann
utterances.text: We really appreciate the opportunity to be here today and really grateful to the New York City Council and under your leadership to hold this hearing and give us the ability to comment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josephine Beckmann
utterances.text: There are significant concerns that we have as one of the 12 fast-track communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josephine Beckmann
utterances.text: The change is an incredible shift in power and resting the Department of City Planning to have final say and review.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josephine Beckmann
utterances.text: We have enjoyed a good working relationship with our local city council members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josephine Beckmann
utterances.text: We have four that represent the district and have worked very closely with Councilmember Kayla Santos-Sorso on a neighborhood plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josephine Beckmann
utterances.text: Each community district is unique in density, square miles, buildable space, and CB10 has a total of 14,909 rent-stabilized units.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josephine Beckmann
utterances.text: We are very concerned about displacement through future rezonings without proper planning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josephine Beckmann
utterances.text: Recent interaction with developers during ULERP really highlighted Councilman Carr's concern about pro forma review, essentially developers feeling that we're no longer part of the process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josephine Beckmann
utterances.text: Community district 10 should not be evaluated solely on one housing production metric without accounting for the realities of our existing built environment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josephine Beckmann
utterances.text: infrastructure, utility, and sewer load, school seat deficits, and transportation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josephine Beckmann
utterances.text: CB10 has a tremendous school seat deficit, still about 4,000, while we've already constructed five new schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josephine Beckmann
utterances.text: Our sewer infrastructure is also antiquated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josephine Beckmann
utterances.text: We are one district that has one of the 14 wastewater treatment plants, which covers five community districts and a conveyance system that is old.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josephine Beckmann
utterances.text: We recently had funding, maybe not recently, seven years awaiting for new sewers in the district that was already adopted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josephine Beckmann
utterances.text: And we're just hoping that the city council continues to work with the boards and really understand the new role of the city planning commission in this process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Josephine Beckmann
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you, Josephine Rochelle.

chapters.summary: She says she has lived in rent-stabilized apartment for 41 years, faced 19 eviction attempts, asks council to protect seniors and enforce housing code.
chapters.title: Rochelle Thompson testifies on senior tenant harassment and eviction

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rochelle Thompson
utterances.text: Oh, all right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rochelle Thompson
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Rochelle Thompson, and I am known as the First Lady of Jazz in Harlem, USA, the continent that I love.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rochelle Thompson
utterances.text: I've lived in my rent-stabilized apartment for 41 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rochelle Thompson
utterances.text: They have tried to evict me 19 times, every entity, five of them that's come into the building.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rochelle Thompson
utterances.text: They have tried to take me to court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rochelle Thompson
utterances.text: Recently, they tried to do a holdover, and I was in HP court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rochelle Thompson
utterances.text: I did win my court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rochelle Thompson
utterances.text: battle, but in the HP court, Judge Leslie A.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rochelle Thompson
utterances.text: Granger signed a warrant for my eviction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rochelle Thompson
utterances.text: So I reported her to the Judicial Oversight Committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rochelle Thompson
utterances.text: I'm here today to let the council know, as seniors, we are targeted, we are not listened to, we're constantly in court, we cannot get counsel.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rochelle Thompson
utterances.text: I had to face three

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rochelle Thompson
utterances.text: landlord attorneys alone, but I kicked their you-know-what.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rochelle Thompson
utterances.text: So I am hoping that the council will take in consideration that our leases or recertification

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rochelle Thompson
utterances.text: should be automatically done, that we're, again, there's a cap on how many times they can take us to court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rochelle Thompson
utterances.text: I've been down here before and spoke about this four times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rochelle Thompson
utterances.text: Please listen to the senior citizens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rochelle Thompson
utterances.text: Please be proactive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rochelle Thompson
utterances.text: Please, if we are in class C violations with mixing valves and scaffolding in front of the building,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rochelle Thompson
utterances.text: please have the code enforcement from HPD just come into the building, go into the basement, and fix the mixing valves before there is a fire in the building.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rochelle Thompson
utterances.text: Thank you for letting me speak.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: And thank you to this panel for testifying today.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: The next panel will consist of Christina Weggs, Zenip Turin, Andrea Goldwyn, and Emma Bartley.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: And we'll be in first with Andrea Goldman.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Take your time, Andre.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: I'm not rushing you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: I don't want you to trip.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You can begin, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Andrea.

chapters.summary: She opposes fast track and fair housing growth strategy, says they will lead to demolition of existing affordable housing and remove public participation, and concerns about historic districts.
chapters.title: Andrea Goldwyn of New York Landmarks Conservancy testifies on fast track and historic districts

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Goldwyn
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Riley and Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Goldwyn
utterances.text: I'm Andrea Goldwyn speaking on behalf of the New York Landmarks Conservancy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Goldwyn
utterances.text: The Conservancy has a long record of supporting existing housing that is affordable and the conversion of underutilized buildings into more affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Goldwyn
utterances.text: Like others, we support comprehensive planning that creates certainty for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Goldwyn
utterances.text: But we can't support the affordable housing fast track and the fair housing growth strategy as incorporated into block by block.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Goldwyn
utterances.text: These plans will lead to the demolition of existing affordable housing in favor of unlimited new construction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Goldwyn
utterances.text: And they remove public participation from the land use process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Goldwyn
utterances.text: Most residents and council members welcome affordable housing, but have questions about adding massive new development without any support for improving infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Goldwyn
utterances.text: The plans that the administration proposes forget the lessons of the past, when government czars such as Robert Moses had boundless power and neighborhoods were routinely demolished.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Goldwyn
utterances.text: Many neighborhoods with historic districts are already the densest and most crowded.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Goldwyn
utterances.text: They are almost completely built out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Goldwyn
utterances.text: The fair housing growth targets will put more development pressure on these historic districts and surrounding areas, especially the older, smaller buildings that often contain smaller, less expensive apartments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Goldwyn
utterances.text: The report calls for enormous increases in the rate of housing unit growth in the upper echelons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Goldwyn
utterances.text: East and Upper West Sides.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Goldwyn
utterances.text: But as Councilmember Brewer has pointed out here and elsewhere, CD7 on the Upper West Side contains NYCHA units, temporary supportive housing, SROs, and subsidized housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Goldwyn
utterances.text: It had a net loss of over 15,000 rent-stabilized units over 15 years, which the city and state did not stop.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Goldwyn
utterances.text: The Conservancy supports appropriate new construction in historic districts, and we've testified in favor of many such proposals at the Landmarks Commission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Goldwyn
utterances.text: However, adding the equivalent of another borough across the entire city or several hundred super tall towers in any neighborhood will put untenable strains on infrastructure and services, and it will lead to the demolition of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Goldwyn
utterances.text: existing housing that defines New York's diverse neighborhoods and diverse, excuse me, unique identity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrea Goldwyn
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to present the Conservancy's views.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Kevin C. Riley
utterances.text: Next we'll hear from Emma.

chapters.summary: She supports affordable housing but concerns about high market-rate targets incentivizing demolitions, and says city's measure of housing growth overlooks conversions and rehab.
chapters.title: Emma Bartley of Historic Districts Council testifies on preservation and affordability

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Emma Bartley
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Emma Bartley
utterances.text: My name is Emma Bartley, and I'm the policy manager from the Historic Districts Council, the citywide advocate for New York's historic neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Emma Bartley
utterances.text: I'm here today to express HTC's comments and concerns about the fair housing growth strategy and aspects of the affordable housing fast track.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Emma Bartley
utterances.text: HDC supports the goal of expanding the city's affordable housing opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Emma Bartley
utterances.text: We have strongly supported housing growth through our advocacy, including testifying in support of large-scale affordable housing developments within historic districts, supporting the proposed South of Prospect neighborhood rezoning,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Emma Bartley
utterances.text: and recently launching our new initiative, Preserving Affordability, which seeks to unlock more historic tax credits to rehab historic affordable rental buildings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Emma Bartley
utterances.text: However, while we support the goals of the growth strategy, we have concerns about its approach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Emma Bartley
utterances.text: We are particularly concerned that high, largely market rate housing production targets could incentivize demolitions across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Emma Bartley
utterances.text: This concern is compounded by the affordable housing fast track's inclusion of already densely developed neighborhoods like the Upper West Side, where vacant or developable land is limited.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Emma Bartley
utterances.text: This is not just a preservation issue, but an affordability issue, as older buildings containing rent-regulated or naturally occurring affordable housing are particularly vulnerable to redevelopment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Emma Bartley
utterances.text: A comprehensive housing strategy must better account for existing density and displacement risk when setting neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Emma Bartley
utterances.text: head targets, while also establishing a clear plan to preserve existing affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Emma Bartley
utterances.text: We also wish to echo a point recently made by Council Member Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Emma Bartley
utterances.text: The city's measure of housing growth appears to be flawed because it focuses on new construction, while overlooking housing created or retained through rehab, adaptive reuse, and conversions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Emma Bartley
utterances.text: The New York Times recently reported that since 2023, the city has permitted over 19,000 units to be created through conversion projects.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Emma Bartley
